| 3 | 6 | 12 |
| 4 | 8 | 16 |
| 5 | 10 | 20 |
| 6 | 12 | 24 |
| 7 | 14 | 28 |
| 8 | 16 | 32 |
| 9 | 18 | 36 |
| 10 | 20 | 40 |

records.name: Running
records.text: On your Turn, you can use your Action to sprint. This requires an Average (+2 SL) Athletics Test, and the distance covered is in addition to your Move this round. You sprint your Run movement + SL in yards (see the Movement Table for your Run movement). So, a character with Move 4 who rolled -2 SL would sprint an additional 14 yards (16-2=14).

records.name: 1: Roll to Hit
records.text:
Melee: Make an Opposed Melee Test against your target. The combatant with the higher SL wins (see page 130).

Ranged: Make a Ranged Test using your weapon. On a success, you hit. On a failure, your attack misses.

In both melee and ranged combat, rolling double on a success is a Critical Hit, while a failed double is a Fumble (see Critical Hits and Fumbles below).

Summary: Test to hit your opponent with your weapon. This Test is Opposed in melee.

records.name: 2: Determine Hit Location
records.text:
If your attack hits, reverse the digits of your successful hit roll and compare the result to the Hit Locations table. For example, a roll of 23 becomes 32, striking the right arm.

Creatures with unusual anatomies may use different Hit Location tables (see Chapter 12: Bestiary).

| d100 | Location |
| --- | --- |
| 01–09 | Head |
| 10–24 | Left Arm (or Secondary Arm) |
| 25–44 | Right Arm (or Primary Arm) |
| 45–79 | Body |
| 80–89 | Left Leg |
| 90–00 | Right Leg |

records.name: 3: Determine Damage
records.text:
Each weapon has a Weapon Damage (see pages 301 and 303). This is usually your modified Strength Bonus for melee weapons, or a fixed number for ranged weapons.

The Damage you deal on a successful attack is your weapon’s Weapon Damage plus the SL of your attack. For Melee Attacks, use the final SL of the Opposed Melee Test. For Ranged Attacks, use the SL of your successful Ranged Test.

Summary: Damage = Weapon Damage + SL

records.name: 4: Apply Damage
records.text:
Subtract your target’s Toughness Bonus and the Armour Points protecting the struck Hit Location from your Damage. The remainder is the number of Wounds they lose.

An attack that inflicts Damage always causes at least 1 Wound, even if Toughness Bonus and Armour reduce the total to 0 or less.

You cannot reduce Wounds below 0. If the Wounds lost exceed the target’s remaining Wounds, they suffer a Critical Wound (see page 171).

Summary: Wounds Lost (minimum 1) = Damage − Toughness Bonus − Armour Points

records.name: Damaged Armour
records.text:
As blows rain down on your armour, it can be damaged, possibly permanently. Whenever you are instructed to damage a piece of armour, reduce the AP in the damaged Hit location by 1.

If this lowers the AP to 0 in that location, the armour there is rendered useless.

records.name: Damaged Weapons
records.text: some Fumble results (see page 165) or spells may damage your weapon. For each point of Damage your weapon receives, reduce its Damage by –1. If the Damage is reduced to +0 (or +sB + 0), the weapon is mangled beyond all recognition, and now counts as an Improvised Weapon. If an Improvised Weapon is damaged, it is considered useless for melee combat.

records.name: Critical Hits
records.text:
Any successful Melee or Ranged Test that rolls a double is a Critical Hit, even if you are defending in an Opposed Test.

A Critical Hit inflicts an immediate Critical Wound (see page 171). Beyond that, resolve the attack normally, including calculating SL and determining the winner of any Opposed Test.

records.name: Fumbles
records.text:
Any failed Melee or Ranged Test that rolls a double is a Fumble.

By default, you drop your weapon and must spend your next Action retrieving it. Alternatively, the GM may roll on the Oops! Table.

records.name: Misfires!
records.text:
If you are using a Blackpowder, Engineering, or Explosive weapon and roll 99 or 00, your weapon Misfires: roll on the Misfire Table instead of the Oops! Table.

### Misfire Table

| d10 | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 1–8 | The weapon fails to fire. If a gun, it must be reloaded. If an explosive, it is a dud. |
| 9–10 | Catastrophe! The weapon explodes, dealing full Damage to your primary arm with +0 SL for the hit. |

records.name: Oops! Table
records.text:
| 1d10 | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 1–2 | You catch a part of your anatomy (we recommend you play this for laughs) — lose 1 Wound, ignoring Toughness Bonus or Armour Points. |
| 3–4 | Your melee weapon jars badly, or ranged weapon malfunctions or slightly breaks — your weapon suffers 1 Damage. Next Round, you will act last regardless of Combat Initiative order, Talents, or special rules as you recover (see page 161). |
| 5–6 | Your manoeuvre was misjudged, leaving you out of position, or you lose grip of a ranged weapon. Next Round, your Action suffers a penalty of −1 SL. |
| 7 | You stumble badly, finding it hard to right yourself. Lose your next Move. |
| 8 | You mishandle your weapon, or you drop your ammunition. Miss your next Action. |
| 9 | You overextend yourself or stumble and twist your ankle. Suffer −1 SL when using one of your legs (randomly determined) for 1d10 Rounds. This counts as a Critical Wound. |
| 10 | You completely mess up, hitting 1 random ally in range using your rolled units die to determine the SL of the hit. If that is not possible, you somehow hit yourself in the face and gain a Stunned Condition (see page 186). |

records.name: Opposed Tests and Fumbles
records.text:
In an Opposed Test, you can Fumble and still win if your SL is higher than your opponent’s. This is fine, and not a little hilarious, as you ineffectually tussle with your even worse opponent, potentially injuring yourself in the process.

Example: Molli attacks with her dagger and rolls 66, a Fumble with -3 SL. Her opponent rolls 92 for -5 SL. Molli wins the Opposed Test by 2 SL, but still suffers the effects of her Fumble, rolling on the Oops! Table to see what happens.

records.name: Ranged Combat
records.text:
There are some extra considerations that apply to ranged attacks:

• Ranged Attacks cannot normally be opposed with Melee Skills. At Point Blank Range (page 166), however, the target may oppose the attack with Dodge.

• You cannot make Ranged Attacks while Engaged, unless your weapon has the Pistol Quality (see page 305).

• If you make a Ranged Attack against a target you are Engaged with, they may oppose the attack with any Melee Skill.

records.name: Combat Modifiers
records.text:
Combat Tests are usually Challenging (+0 SL). Circumstances may grant an SL modifier or penalty to Ranged or Melee Tests.

These modifiers apply to Attack Tests only, not to Tests made to oppose an attack. If an attacker gains Advantage on a Melee Test due to outnumbering their target, the defender does not automatically suffer Disadvantage on a Melee Test made to parry that blow simply because they are outnumbered.

### Ranged Attack Modifiers — Add All That Apply

| Circumstance | Modifier |
| --- | --- |
| Size is larger than you / Monstrous | +1 SL / +2 SL |
| Range is Short / Point Blank | +1 SL / +2 SL |
| Target is Surprised | +1 SL |
| You spent an Action last Turn aiming at the target | +1 SL |
| Target is smaller than you / Tiny | −1 SL / −2 SL |
| Range is Long / Extreme | −1 SL / −2 SL |
| Target is in cover or Prone | −1 SL |
| Fog or poor lighting / rain and wind / extreme weather or pitch blackness | −1 SL / −2 SL / −3 SL |
| Attacker moved before firing | −1 SL |

### Melee Attack Modifiers

| Circumstance | Modifier |
| --- | --- |
| Target is outnumbered / surrounded | +1 SL / +2 SL |
| Target is Surprised | +1 SL |
| Target is Prone or attacker has high ground | +1 SL |
| Target is Entangled | +1 SL |
| Attacker is in mud, water, or difficult terrain | −1 SL |
| Attacker is in an enclosed space with a weapon of Average / greater reach | −1 SL / −2 SL |
| Attacker is Prone | −1 SL |
| Attacker’s weapon is in the off-hand | −2 SL |
| Defender has high ground | −1 SL |

records.name: Melee Weapon Group Special Rules
records.text:
Some Melee Weapon Groups have special rules.

• On foot, you may use a two handed Cavalry Weapon with Melee (Two-handed) with no penalty, if you prefer.

• Single-handed Cavalry Weapons count as Improvised

Weapons when on foot.

• You may use a Fencing Weapon with Melee (Basic), but cannot use its Qualities when doing so.

• Using a Flail without any Advances in Melee (Flail) causes such weapons to gain the Dangerous Flaw.

records.name: Melee Weapon Reach
records.text:
Weapon reach (page 300) has the following impacts:

• When opposing a Melee Attack Test, you gain +1 SL if the attacker’s weapon is shorter than yours.

• If your weapon is Very Long, you can Engage enemies up to 4 yards away, or 6 yards if its Reach is Massive.

records.name: Weapon Groups
records.text:
Knowing how to swing a sword doesn’t necessarily make you an expert with a spear, and the technique and understanding required to use a bow is quite different from the skills required to use a blackpowder weapon. When you use a weapon, roll against the appropriate Skill Specialisation, such as Melee (Basic) or Ranged (Blackpowder). Weapons are broken into various Weapon Groups, each tied to a Skill Specialisation.

If you are using a Melee Weapon from a Weapon Group you have no Advances in, you may still Test against your Weapon Skill. In such a case, you do not benefit from its Qualities (page 304), but your attack still suffers from the weapon’s Flaws.

Ranged Weapons are typically more complicated, and you cannot make Ranged Attacks with a weapon from a Weapon Group you have no Advances in, save for a few exceptions:

• Ranged (Engineering) can be used with Blackpowder and Explosive weapons.

• You may also use Engineering Weapons with Ranged (Blackpowder), but such Tests are always at least Hard (-2 SL).

• You may make a Ballistic Skill Test to attack with Crossbow and Throwing weapons, but these attacks are always at least Difficult (-1 SL).

records.name: Aimed Shots
records.text: If you spend an Action aiming at your target, you gain +1 SL on your next ranged attack against them. You must have your ranged weapon in hand to aim, and the bonus is lost if you do anything else before taking your shot, such as moving or defending yourself.

records.name: Called Shots
records.text: If you wish to target a specific Hit Location, you take a -2 SL penalty to your Attack Test. If you succeed, the attack hits whichever location you wish.

records.name: Grappling
records.text:
Instead of inflicting damage with an unarmed attack, you can attempt to Grapple and immobilise your opponent. You must declare this is your intent before rolling to hit your opponent. If you win the Opposed Test, you and your opponent are Grappling and your opponent gains an Entangled Condition (page 186). If you begin your Turn Grappling, you must make an Opposed Strength Test for your Action. If you win, you can do one of the following:

•  Deal SB + SL Damage using your Strength Test roll to determine the Hit Location affected. You ignore any Armour Points as you wrench arms and pull muscles.

•  Give your opponent an Entangled Condition, plus one more for each SL after the first.

•  Remove an Entangled Condition from yourself, plus one more for each SL after the first.

records.name: Helpless Targets
records.text:
When making a Melee Attack (or a Ranged Attack at Point Blank Range) against a sleeping, unconscious, or otherwise Helpless target, you choose the result of your attack roll instead of rolling. You automatically hit and may choose the Hit Location if you score a Critical Hit.

If the GM prefers a more lethal game, any such attack against a Helpless target simply kills them.

If you can Oppose an attack but choose not to, you count as Helpless.

records.name: Outnumbering
records.text: You outnumber an opponent only if your side has at least twice as many Engaged combatants as theirs. Only combatants Engaged with one another count when determining this. If there is any doubt, the GM decides who outnumbers whom.

records.name: Shooting into Melee
records.text:
Ranged attacks against Engaged targets suffer Disadvantage. If this causes an attack that would otherwise have hit to miss, you instead hit one of the target’s Engaged opponents, chosen at random by the GM.

If you do not care who you hit, treat the melee as a group instead (see Shooting into a Group).

records.name: Shooting into a Group
records.text: Shooting into a group of half a dozen or more grants Advantage, but you cannot choose which member of the group you hit, including any allies mixed into the fray. On a successful attack, the GM randomly determines the target from among the likely candidates.

records.name: Surrounded
records.text: A target is surrounded if they have no route of escape. This usually requires at least three attackers, though two may suffice in a confined space such as a tunnel or narrow hallway.

records.name: Two-weapon Fighting
records.text:
Some warriors fight with a weapon in each hand, such as a sword and sword-breaker, or an axe and pistol.

When fighting with two weapons:

•  You may wield any two one-handed weapons.

•  After attacking with one weapon, you may spend Momentum (page 168) to immediately attack with the weapon in your other hand.

•  Attacks made with your off hand suffer -2 SL.

Note: The Ambidextrous and Dual Wielder Talents can mitigate penalties associated with two-weapon fighting.

records.name: Unarmed Combat
records.text: Not every fight in WFRP involves guns or swords. Many conflicts are settled with good old-fashioned fisticuffs. A successful Melee (Brawling) Test for unarmed combat is handled in the same way as any other combat Test, but you have one extra option: you may enter a Grapple!

records.name: Undamaging and Unarmed Attacks
records.text: For those lacking claws, fangs, or some other natural enchancement, attacks made without a weapon are Undamaging. Any AP the target posses are doubled, attacks do not inflict a minimum of 1 Wound, and, if a Critical Wound is inflicted, roll twice on the Critical Wound table and choose the lower result.

records.name: Gaining Momentum
records.text:
Whenever you make a successful Opposed Melee Test against an opponent in combat, you gain Momentum. You either have Momentum or you don’t, so gaining Momentum twice has no additional effect.

When you have Momentum, you gain Advantage (page 130) on any Melee Test you make. You gain this benefit even if you are attacking a character other than the one you gained Momentum ‘from’. The benefits of Momentum do not apply to any other Tests.

records.name: Losing Momentum
records.text: You lose Momentum when you fail a Melee Test — including losing an Opposed Test where you gained some SL, but not enough to beat your opponent — suffer Damage, or have a Condition inflicted upon you. You also lose any Momentum when combat ends, or there is otherwise a pause in fighting. Some Talents and Creature Traits also allow you to spend Momentum to gain certain benefits, such as making an attack with a secondary weapon or vomiting acidic bile upon one’s foes.

records.name: Momentum
records.text:
Experienced fighters know that a warrior who strikes first and strikes well is likely to win a fight. In combat, Momentum is gained by striking an opponent with a Melee Attack, and can later be used to maintain a dominant position.

All characters, including NPCs, use Momentum. It is up to each player to keep track of whether they have Momentum or not, while the GM keeps track of NPCs.

Gaining Momentum

Whenever you make a successful Opposed Melee Test against an opponent in combat, you gain Momentum. You either have Momentum or you don’t, so gaining Momentum twice has no additional effect.

When you have Momentum, you gain Advantage (page 130) on any Melee Test you make. You gain this benefit even if you are attacking a character other than the one you gained Momentum ‘from’. The benefits of Momentum do not apply to any other Tests.

Losing Momentum

You lose Momentum when you fail a Melee Test — including losing an Opposed Test where you gained some SL, but not enough to beat your opponent — suffer Damage, or have a Condition inflicted upon you. You also lose any Momentum when combat ends, or there is otherwise a pause in fighting. Some Talents and Creature Traits also allow you to spend Momentum to gain certain benefits, such as making an attack with a secondary weapon or vomiting acidic bile upon one’s foes.

Momentum And Extra Attacks

No matter the circumstances, a character or NPC may only spend Momentum to make one additional attack each Turn, even if they gain Momentum again after doing so.

records.name: Momentum and Extra Attacks
records.text: No matter the circumstances, a character or NPC may only spend Momentum to make one additional attack each Turn, even if they gain Momentum again after doing so.

records.name: Mounted Combat
records.text:
Riding into combat, sword swinging, guns blazing, is not only terrifying for those on the receiving end, it also brings bonuses to the rider. Mounted combat uses the same rules as any other combat, with the following additions:

• For the purposes of their Move, riders count as having the Movement Attribute of their mount. Further, riders take Ride Tests as Free Actions for any Tests to Sprint, Leap, Charge, or similar, and use their mount’s Movement Attribute.

• Any Melee Test made with a Cavalry weapon by a rider against a target smaller than their mount gains Advantage.

• You choose whether to target a rider or their mount. If you attempt to hit the rider in melee, touch them, or similar, you suffer Disadvantage on the Test if you are smaller Size than the mount (see page 360), unless your weapon has a reach of Long or greater.

• A mount without the Skittish Trait (see page 361) is effectively another combatant, and may use its own Action to attack targets.

• When Charging, you may count as having your mount’s Strength Bonus for the purpose of calculating Weapon Damage.

• When riding, you suffer Disadvantage on Dodge Tests unless you have the Trick Rider Talent.

Note: Most mounts are bigger than Characters, meaning they may cause Fear and gain other combat advantages as explained on page 360.

records.name: Scatter
records.text:
On a failed Ranged (Throwing) Test, roll 1d10 and consult the following diagram to see where your weapon lands. ‘T’ marks the Target.

1 2 3 4 T 5 6 7 8

A roll of 1–8 provides a direction: roll 2d10 to determine the distance the weapon scatters in yards — it scatters no more than half the distance between you and the target. A roll of 9 and the weapon lands at your feet. A 10, and it lands at your target’s feet.

Scatter can be used whenever a random direction is required.

records.name: Drowning and Suffocation
records.text:
If prepared, you can hold your breath for Toughness Bonus x 10 seconds without a Test. After that, you may start to suffocate or drown. If you are unprepared and suddenly deprived of air, you will start to suffocate immediately.

Each Round you are being suffocated, you lose 1 Wound. Should you reach 0 Wounds, you immediately receive the Unconscious Condition. After that, you will die of suffocation or drowning in Toughness Bonus Rounds.

records.name: Falling
records.text: When you fall, you suffer 3 Damage for each yard, reduced by your Toughness Bonus, but not any Armour you may be wearing. If you lose more Wounds than your Toughness Bonus, make a Challenging (+0 SL) Endurance Test. If you fail, you fall Prone and suffer an immediate Critical Wound to your Leg. If the result is an Astounding Failure, take an additional Critical Wound to a random location as well. If you are intentionally jumping down rather than falling, you may mitigate the Damage (see Jumping Down page 157).

records.name: Intimidate in Combat
records.text:
You can threaten a foe in the hopes of leaving them demoralised. As an Action make an Intimidate Test opposed by the target’s Cool. If successful, the target Fears you, treating you as having a Fear rating of 1, plus 1 more for each SL after the first.

Intimidating a group of foes raises the Difficulty of the Test to Hard (-2 SL). When fighting a well-led enemy, the Test is Opposed by the Leadership Skill of whoever is in charge. When fighting a disorganised rabble, the Test is Opposed by the lowest Cool among the foe, as fear easily spreads among such groups.

records.name: Leadership in Combat
records.text:
A Leadership Test allows you to issue orders to NPCs clearly and with authority. If you’re attempting to order your natural subordinates — a noble commanding serfs, or a sergeant commanding their troops — commands are usually unopposed. If there is no natural hierarchy in place, or the order is particularly challenging — such as ordering your soldiers to charge a hydra head on — the Test is Opposed by your targets’ Cool. If you are contesting another’s authority, make an Opposed Leadership Test — the orders of the winner will be followed, though such disagreements are usually terrible for morale.

You may use Leadership to encourage an ally, as long as you don’t have the Broken Condition. As a Free Action, make a Leadership Test to remove a Broken Condition from one ally of your choice, plus one additional Broken Condition from that ally or another for each SL after the first.

Leadership can also be used to transfer Momentum. As a Free Action, lose Momentum to make a Leadership Test. If you succeed, you may grant Momentum to one ally of your choice.

records.name: Exposure
records.text:
Every 4 hours spent in a difficult environment — such as subzero temperatures, a hot desert, or a howling storm — requires you to take an Endurance Test. Extreme environments require a Test every 2 hours.

Cold: Your first failure inflicts Disadvantage on Tests based on Ballistic Skill, Agility, and Dexterity. The second failure inflicts Disadvantage on all Tests. Subsequent failures cause 1d10 Damage, ignoring Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds, you do not suffer a Critical Wound, but immediately take the Unconscious Condition. You will die in Toughness Bonus hours unless you are somehow warmed up. Certain Trappings may provide bonuses or penalties to these Tests, for example a coat (page 309).

Heat: Your first failure inflicts Disadvantage on Tests based on Intelligence and Willpower, and adds a Fatigued Condition. The second failure inflicts Disadvantage on all Tests, and adds another Fatigued Condition. Subsequent failures cause 1d10 Damage ignoring Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds, you do not suffer a Critical Wound, but immediately take the Unconscious Condition. You will die in Toughness Bonus hours unless you are somehow cooled off. Stripping off all armour grants +1 SL on Endurance Tests to resist exposure to heat.

records.name: Healing Wounds
records.text: At the end of each day, make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test. If successful, you recover Wounds equal to the SL + your Toughness Bonus. If the day was spent restfully, you recover a further number of Wounds equal to your Toughness Bonus even if you failed this Test.

records.name: Thirst and Starvation
records.text:
Running out of provisions can be bad. Running out of water is worse. Endurance Tests to withstand thirst and hunger become increasingly difficult (cumulative -1 SL for each Test after the first). Characters without food and water cannot heal Wounds or recover Fatigued naturally.

Water: Every day without water requires you to take an Endurance Test. The first failed Test inflicts Disadvantage on Tests based on Intelligence, Willpower, and Fellowship. Second and subsequent failures inflict Disadvantage on all Tests, and cause 1d10 Damage ignoring Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds, you do not suffer a Critical Wound, but reduce your Movement to 1, and you will die in Toughness Bonus days, unless you get something to drink.

Food: Every 2 days without food requires an Endurance Test. The first failed Test inflicts Disadvantage on Tests based on Strength and Toughness. Second and subsequent failures inflict Disadvantage on all Tests, and cause 1d10 Damage ignoring Armour Points. If you reach 0 Wounds, you do not suffer a Critical Wound, but permanently reduce your Toughness by 1d10. See Characteristic Loss, page 177.

records.name: Using the Heal Skill
records.text:
You, or another Character, can use the Heal skill to recover more Wounds, so long as they have access to bandages, poultices, or other medical supplies. A successful Heal Test recovers Intelligence Bonus + SL Wounds. The difficulty of the Test is determined by the circumstances and the nature of the injury — during Combat it is never easier than Challenging (+0 SL). A patient can only benefit from one Heal roll per incident in which they lost Wounds, such as a fight, fall, or unfortunate accident involving the graf’s horse.

A fumbled Heal Test inflicts 1d10 Wounds, but cannot reduce the target below 1 Wound.

records.name: Wounds
records.text: Wound loss represents minor cuts, bruises, and depleted reserves of energy. Wounds are lost by sustaining Damage (page 164). The lowest number of Wounds you can ever have is 0. If you would be taken to negative Wounds, you instead suffer a Critical Wound.

records.name: Critical Wounds
records.text:
Critical Wounds are severe, and include broken bones, torn muscles, internal injuries, and sundered flesh. Critical Wounds are debilitating and dangerous. Gain too many and you risk death.

There are two ways to receive a Critical Wound. One is to suffer a Critical Hit, the other is to incur any Damage that would reduce your Wounds below 0.

Inflicting Critical Wounds on an Opponent with 0 Wounds If Damage would reduce a character to below 0 Wounds, instead reduce them to 0 Wounds and inflict a Critical Wound. Roll a d100 on the relevant Critical Wounds table for the struck Location (pages 173–176). When rolling on the Critical Wounds table, add +10 to the result for every Wound inflicted beyond what was needed to reduce them to 0 Wounds.

Inflicting Critical Wounds with Critical Hits Any Critical on a Melee or Ranged Test, whether attacking or defending, is a Critical Hit and inflicts a Critical Wound. For a Critical Wound caused by a Critical Hit, do not reverse your attack roll to find out the Location of your strike as you would do for a normal hit. Instead, roll a d100 again to work out where your hit landed (see page 164), then roll a d100 again on the relevant Critical Wounds table for that Location.

Attack Tests that both result in a Critical Hit and which inflict Damage that would reduce Wounds below zero inflict two Critical Wounds — one inflicted to a hit location determined by reversing the roll, and an additional one inflicted to a random hit location, as explained above.

records.name: Magic, Alchemy, and Healing
records.text: Spells, Blessings, and some rare concoctions (page 314) can also heal Wounds, though such means are all either rare, expensive, or both.

records.name: Death
records.text:
Death can result directly from a Critical Wound or if a Character succumbs to many injuries. If you have more Critical Wounds than your Toughness Bonus, you are at risk of death. In such circumstances, should you incur the Unconscious Condition from an attack, Spell, Bleeding Condition, or the effects of a Critical Wound, you begin to succumb to your injuries. You will perish after Toughness Bonus rounds unless you are healed of one or more Critical Wounds or the Unconscious Condition is removed.

Sudden Death As the GM, you may not wish to track the details of injuries for all participants, and can instead simply determine if someone is dead or not using the Sudden Death rules. In this case, when a target reaches 0 Wounds, the GM can simply declare them dead or unconscious.

Sudden Death is useful for determining the fate of background NPCs such as brigands or low-tier cultists, but it should not be used to determine the fate of Player Characters, or for NPCs with the Luck Talent.

records.name: Healing Critical Wounds
records.text: If you have received any Critical Wounds, you are said to be Critically Wounded. Critical Wounds can be very serious. Refer to the appropriate Critical Wounds table to see exactly what penalties and Injuries (page 176) you suffer for any Critical Wounds sustained. Critical Wounds do not count as healed until all Conditions they inflict are removed and all non-permanent negative modifiers are resolved. When you are Critically Wounded, you may still heal your Wounds using the normal rules.

records.name: Medical Attention
records.text:
Several Critical Wound results and conditions cannot be resolved until you receive some kind of Medical Attention. All of the following count as Medical Attention, as could other means and effects, at the GM’s discretion.

• Successful use of the Heal Skill.

• Application of a Bandage, Healing Poultice, or similar.

• Successful use of a Prayer or Spell that heals Wounds.

records.name: Surgery
records.text: Some wounds are beyond simple stitching and foul-smelling poultices. If you suffer a Critical Wound where surgery is required to attend to it (marked ‘Surgery’), you suffer the marked penalties until you visit an appropriately trained doktor or barber-surgeon, or somehow source a magical or divine surgery equivalent. A character with the Surgery Talent can treat such a Critical Wound by making a Challenging (+0 SL) Heal Test.

records.name: Broken Bones
records.text: Small fractures may heal on their own accord, but severe breaks, with bone protruding at odd angles from the flesh, are a different matter entirely. If you suffer a Broken Bone, it will be marked as Minor or Major.

records.name: Amputated Parts
records.text: Many of the more severe Critical Wounds result in the loss of a body part, such as fingers, hands, feet, or even a whole leg! Should a Character suffer more than one severed body part, it is probably time to start looking for an appropriate replacement to mitigate any possible penalties (see Chapter 11: Consumer Guide). Whenever you suffer a Critical Wound marked ‘Amputation (Difficulty)’, you must pass an Endurance Test (the Difficulty is marked in the parentheses) or gain the Prone Condition. On a Failure (-1 SL) or worse, you also gain a Stunned Condition; on an Impressive Failure (-4 SL or worse), gain the Unconscious Condition. All amputations require Surgery to heal properly, the associated Critical Wound does not count as healed until you visit a surgeon. See Surgery on page 172.

records.name: Torn Muscles
records.text:
Sprains or tears to your muscles or ligaments result in significant pain and possible loss of use depending upon the severity, which will be marked as Minor or Major.

Minor One of your muscles is sprained or torn, resulting in impaired capabilities and much pain. Suffer a penalty of -1 SL to all Tests involving the Location. If a leg is hit, also halve your Movement.

Healing: The muscle will partially heal in 30 - Toughness Bonus days. Successful use of the Heal Skill reduces the time by 1 day, plus a further day per SL after the first — you can gain this benefit once.

Major One of your muscles or some important tendons have been severely damaged, resulting in extreme pain and a significant loss in capability of the afflicted limb. Suffer the same effects as Torn Muscle (Minor), but the penalties are -2 SL to all Tests.

Healing: The muscle will partially heal in 30 - Toughness Bonus days, after which the penalty for using the limb reduces to -1 SL to all relevant Tests. The muscle will completely heal after another 30 - Toughness Bonus days. Use of the Heal Skill does little but inform you of the extent of the damage.

records.name: Arm
records.text: Use the rules for lost hand, but you cannot strap a shield to the arm since you do not have one.

records.name: Ear
records.text: Losing an ear is painful, but does not lead to any measurable penalty. Should you have the bad luck to lose both your ears, you suffer Disadvantage on all hearing-based Perception Tests.

records.name: Eye
records.text: Losing an eye is horrendous, but you soon learn to compensate. Should you have the misfortune to lose both eyes, you suffer Disadvantage on all Tests influenced by sight and opponents gain Advantage on Tests made to hit you in melee.

records.name: Fingers
records.text: Losing a finger results in lessened grip, you suffer a -1 SL penalty to all Tests using the hand in question per finger lost. Once 4 or more fingers are lost on a hand, use the rules for a severed hand.

records.name: Foot
records.text: Losing a foot reduces your Movement by half, rounding up, permanently. Further, you lose 10 points each of Weapon Skill and Agility, and suffer Disadvantage on all Dodge and Athletics Tests. If you lose a second foot, reduce your Movement to 1, and lose another 5 points of Weapon Skill and Agility. Reduce the Characteristic penalty caused by a lost foot by the number of toes previously severed from that appendage, if any.

records.name: Hand
records.text: You suffer Disadvantage on all Tests that typically rely on the use of two hands and you cannot wield two-handed weapons; however, a shield can be strapped to the injured arm. Should the lost hand be your primary hand, remember that there is a -2 SL penalty to Melee Tests made with weapons using your off-hand. For every 100 XP you spend, you can reduce this penalty by 1 SL as you relearn how to do everything with the other hand. If you lose both hands, you will need to use prosthetics in order to manipulate objects.

records.name: Leg
records.text: Treat this as a lost foot, but you cannot use the Dodge Skill at all.

records.name: Nose
records.text: A loss of a nose is an unsettling injury. This always counts as an Impressive Scar, but the bonus and penalty increase to +2 SL and -2 SL respectively. All Tests involving the sense of smell suffer Disadvantage.

records.name: Teeth
records.text: Loss of teeth may be unsightly and can make eating difficult. For every two teeth you lose, you also suffer a permanent loss of 1 from your Fellowship Characteristic. Further, once more than half your teeth (Humans: 16; Elves: 18; Halflings and Dwarfs: 20) are lost, you find consuming solids significantly more difficult than your peers, doubling eating times, and making some foodstuffs nigh-on impossible to eat, which is largely a matter of roleplaying and narrative description of your actions.

records.name: Black Plague
records.text:
Historians claim that in 1111 IC, rats swarmed across the Empire and the Black Plague followed, wiping out nine in every ten souls. Unexplained outbreaks of the horrendous disease still occur today, and when they do, they invariably bring no-nonsense white nuns. The Cult of Shallya has sworn to do everything in its power to eradicate the foul disease. Ancient laws and rights granted to the Cult allow its members to mark infected areas with white-rope plague cordons, preventing anyone from entering or leaving until the outbreak is contained and all bodies correctly disposed of.

Those who do survive the Black Plague rarely ever contract it again — a small mercy for having endured such a horrendous affliction.

Contraction: Enact an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test for each hour, or part thereof, spent in an area infested with infected fleas, or when exposed to infected fluids. Those who have already survived a bout of the Black Plague Test only once each day, and then with Advantage. Incubation: 1d10 hours Duration: 3d10 days Symptoms: Blight, Buboes, Fever

records.name: Blood Rot
records.text:
Your very blood is diseased, and your heart now pumps sickness through your body. Leeching the rot is the accepted cure, but some doktors instead cut careful incisions near the neck to free the contaminated blood, demanding the patient ingest vast quantities of healthy blood to replace what is lost. Whether the patient accepts such remedies or not, without treatment, Blood Rot is deadly, and often ends in a visit from the Mourners Guild and the Cult of Morr.

Contraction: As a development of another disease or a Critical Wound. Incubation: Instant Duration: 1d10 days Symptoms: Blight, Fever, Malaise

records.name: Disease Format
records.text:
• Name: The name of the disease

• A description of the disease

• Contraction: How the disease is contracted

• Incubation: How long before the victim demonstrates any Symptoms

• Duration: How long the Symptoms of the disease last if untreated. At the end of the duration, the disease will come to an end.

• Symptoms: The effects of the disease on the victim. See Symptoms (page 181) for a list of all the Symptoms and how they affect a Character.

• Permanent: Some diseases are so horrendous they carry permanent consequences. This section is only included if the affliction has such long-term effects.

records.name: Disease and Infection
records.text:
Plague and pestilence — the purview of Nurgle, the Chaos God of disease and despair — are an everyday fact of Old World life. Outbreaks of plague affect all levels of society, although the common folk usually fare the worst. To ward against these terrible infections, most turn to the welcoming arms of Nurgle’s sworn enemy, Shallya, the goddess of mercy and healing. Those actually suffering a disease will often turn to any possible cure, ensuring wise women, herbalists, and travelling doktors are never out of business, even when most peddle quackery rather than true remedies.

A disease can be diagnosed with the Heal Skill. The Difficulty of this Test is determined by how rare the disease is, and if the character has encountered it before.

records.name: Toes
records.text: Loss of toes has an adverse effect on your balance. For each toe lost, suffer a permanent loss of -1 to your Weapon Skill and Agility Characteristics.

records.name: Tongue
records.text: A loss of a tongue leaves you grunting and humming, or relying on sign language, for communication. You automatically fail all Language Tests involving speaking.

records.name: Bloody Flux
records.text:
The Bloody Flux is a persistent problem in the Empire, and widely viewed to be a curse upon the impious by the gods. The foul disease causes its unfortunate victim to evacuate the bowels forcibly and frequently. The Bloody Flux is endemic in the State Armies, where it is commonly claimed to kill more soldiers than any enemy. Typical cures include eating blood pudding to replace lost humours, ‘corking’, and rubbing fats into the afflicted area to lessen the sting.

Contraction: If you fail an Easy (+4 SL) Endurance Test after an infected source enters the mouth. Incubation: 1d10 hours Duration: 1d10 days Symptoms: Fever, Flux, Malaise

records.name: Festering Wound
records.text:
Infected cuts and abrasions are commonplace, meaning many superstitions exist explaining how best to treat them. Poultices fashioned from wrapped leaves and dung, the skin of toads, and dove feathers are common. Most physicians rubbish such talk, and prefer more scientific curatives, such as mixing the gall of a black ox with three spoonfuls of the patient’s urine and half a spoon of sea salt, which is then rubbed into the festering, pus- filled wound. The screams this elicits prove just how effective the remedy is.

Contraction: If you fail an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test after a combat with a creature with the Infected trait (see Chapter 12: Bestiary). You can also develop a Festering Wound from an Infection (page 182). Incubation: 1d10 days, or instantly if developed from another disease or Infection. Duration: 1d10 days Symptoms: Fever, Malaise

records.name: Galloping Trots
records.text:
It is said halfling food will not give you Galloping Trots, a messy affliction all too common in the Empire given just how little care is given to the proper preparation of food. Those suffering digestive distress from the cheap halfling pies on sale across Altdorf would disagree, assuming they could escape the privy for long enough…

Contraction: If you fail an Easy (+4 SL) Endurance Test after an infected source enters the mouth. Incubation: 1d10 hours Duration: 1d10 days Symptoms: Flux, Malaise, Nausea

records.name: Itching Pox
records.text:
Annual outbreaks of Itching Pox afflict most towns and cities of the Empire. The disease, which causes body-wide itchy blisters, is relatively mild, and very rarely has lasting complications, so it concerns few outside worried parents or vain nobles. So common is it, that most temples of Shallya have vials of white paste on hand to relieve the itching of the afflicted.

Contraction: If you fail an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test when contact is made with an infected individual. Incubation: 1d10 days Duration: 1d10 + 7 days Symptoms: Pox Permanent: Once the disease is contracted, you become immune to catching it again.

records.name: Packer’s Pox
records.text:
A common infection amongst hunters, furriers, and traders, Packer’s Pox is contracted from infected cattle and sheep, including their hides and wool, and from the bodies of those killed by the disease. It starts as a small, itchy rash, but soon pink, depressed blisters spread across the whole body, concentrating on the torso and arms. Not the worst of the various poxes plaguing the Empire, but it does linger for a very long time, and can occasionally turn deadly.

Contraction: If you fail an Easy (+4 SL) Endurance Test after any contact with infected animals, hides, or bodies. Incubation: 1d10 days Duration: 5d10 days Symptoms: Pox, Infection

records.name: Ratte Fever
records.text:
Contracted from infected rodents, dreaded Ratte Fever brings inflamed rashes and ulcerations before a fever rises and the body begins to spasm. Though rarely fatal, it is a debilitating disease, and it takes a long time to recover. Common remedies include self-flagellation in Altdorf — which reputedly does bring some relief to the skin infections — and smearing oneself in goat cheese mixed with imported Kislevite ice peppers in Talabheim. In the bigger towns and cities, Ratte Fever is also known as Pie Fever given just how many savoury pasties contain tainted rat in place of more expensive meat.

Contraction: If you fail an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test after any combat when wounded by rodents (including skaven) with the Infected Trait, or you fail an Easy (+4 SL) Endurance Test after an infected source enters your mouth. Incubation: 3d10 + 5 days Duration: 3d10 + 10 days Symptoms: Fever, Malaise, Pox

records.name: Blight
records.text: You are seriously ill and perhaps close to Morr’s Portal as deadly poisons flood your body. Pass an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test daily (normally when you sleep). The first time you fail this Test, you gain an Unconscious Condition that cannot be removed until you are no longer suffering from Blight. The second time you fail this Test, you perish.

records.name: Buboes
records.text:
You have huge swellings of the lymph nodes, possibly in the groin, neck, or armpits. These are enormously painful and may bleed or seep pus. They are disgusting and stink of rot — though cultists of the Lord of Pestilence consider them a sure sign of his favour, believing they hide tiny, growing daemons. Common practice is to lance these terrible expressions of taint to remove whatever nestles within, though doing so often results in Festering Wounds.

Suffer a -1 SL penalty to all physical Tests, and to all Fellowship Tests if the buboes can be seen or smelled. A Heal Test made by a character with the Surgery Talent can lance your buboes, removing the penalty. If the Test is failed, gain a Festering Wound. If your Buboes are lanced, make a Difficult (-1 SL) Endurance Test once per day or more swell into place.

records.name: Convulsions
records.text: Your body periodically spasms or shakes as the infection seemingly uses you like a puppet. Suffer a penalty of -1 SL to all physical Tests as your body convulses beyond your control.

records.name: Coughs and Sneezes
records.text: You intermittently cough or sneeze, spreading your disease to those around you. Up to 1d10 times per session (rolled secretly at the start of the session) the GM may inform you that you feel the urge to cough and sneeze. Either make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test or spend your next Action violently expectorating. Any creatures within 3 yards are exposed to the disease and must Test for Contraction.

records.name: Fever
records.text: Your temperature is high, you sweat and shiver, and find it difficult to keep your cool. Any Agility, Dexterity, or Psychology Tests suffer a penalty of -2 SL.

records.name: Flux
records.text: There’s a rumble and a grumble. Any given situation may be the moment you just have to go to the privy. You are expected to take every opportunity you can to pop off for an essential stop, and this is largely left in your hands. In addition, once per session the GM will let you know that you simply have to go immediately. You have a number of Rounds equal to your Toughness Bonus to get to an appropriate place to relieve yourself, or else suffer the Besmirched Condition.

records.name: Sea Sickness
records.text:
Many folk feel queasy when they first spend time aboard a vessel at sea. Once they get used to the motion of the ocean, Sea Sickness only tends to be a problem when there are high winds or a vigorous swell. Elves are immune to Sea Sickness.

Contraction: Whenever a susceptible Character first undertakes a journey at sea, they must make a Challenging (+0 SL) Endurance Test or suffer Sea Sickness. In rough weather, such Characters should make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test or suffer Sea Sickness. Duration: For Sea Sickness due to being new to seafaring, make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test after each day involving travel at sea. If you pass, you will not suffer this form of Sea Sickness again. For Sea Sickness resulting from rough seas or other temporary effects, make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test every hour. Symptoms: Nausea

records.name: Weevil Cough
records.text:
Tiny mites that infest stores of hay, wheat, or flour can bring about a persistent, hacking cough. A spring of mint held to the nose and mouth can calm the tickle that irritates a sufferer’s throat and lungs, but there is no reliable cure for Weevil Cough.

Contraction: If you fail an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test when contact is made with infected hay, wheat, or flour or fail the same Test when an infected individual coughs in your immediate vicinity (at a rate of about one Test per hour of exposure). Incubation: 1d10 days Duration: 1d10 days Symptoms: Coughs and Sneezes, Malaise

records.name: Cures and Tonics
records.text: A plethora of cures for all manner of ailments are available for sale, though their efficacy varies wildly. See Chapter 11: Consumer Guide for how to purchase medicines. Off-the- shelf cures are often unreliable and an Endurance Test is usually required to see if the medicine has an effect; the Difficulty depends on the nature of the cure and the Symptom, as shown in the table below. A success staves off the Symptom for 1 day. On an Astounding Failure (-6 SL), contract Galloping Trots.

records.name: Gangrene
records.text:
Some part of your flesh is withered and dying, infected with something awful or entirely bereft of blood flow. Roll percentile dice to determine a Hit Location (see page 164). If you roll Head, your nose is affected. If you roll Arm, it is a finger. If you roll Leg, it is a toe. If you roll Body, you suffer a Festering Wound.

If a finger, toe, or your nose is affected, roll an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test each day. If you pass, you hold off the Gangrene; if you fail, it grows worse. If you fail more than Toughness Bonus times, you completely lose all capability with the affected location. If this occurs, use the same rules as Amputation (see pages 177–179).

For as long as you have Gangrene, suffer a -1 SL penalty to all Fellowship Tests.

records.name: Infection
records.text:
You have a wound or open sore that will not heal properly because of an infection, weeping foul-smelling pus. For each Infection Symptom you have, you cannot recover 1 Wound. Every day, make a single Very Easy (+6 SL) Endurance Test or gain a Festering Wound if you do not already have one. If you do have one, the Test is Easy (+4 SL), and if you fail, you contract Blood Rot.

An Infection Symptom caused by lost Wounds is removed once it has caused a Festering Wound, or once you have received treatment for the infection. An Infection Symptom caused by a disease remains until that disease is cured.

records.name: Malaise
records.text: You do not feel at all well. You speak with a nasal tone due to your thick tongue and blocked sinuses, your eyes are rheumy, your nose stuffy, and your ears clogged. You lose the ability to make use of any Acute Sense Talents you possess, and any Language or Perception Tests you make suffer from -2 SL.

records.name: Nausea
records.text: You feel very sick and are prone to vomiting if you move around too quickly. Whenever you spend your Turn involved in strenuous physical activity (such as running, climbing, or fighting), make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test. If you fail, you gain 1 Stunned Condition and may gain the Besmirched Condition due to being sick or instead begin dry heaving if your stomach is empty.

records.name: Pox
records.text:
You are covered in pustules, inflamed swellings, disgusting rashes, or itchy spots, which are unlikely to be your most attractive feature. Poxes are largely a cosmetic issue, resulting in a penalty of -1 SL to Fellowship Tests. Additionally, up to two times per session, the GM may announce that you are suffering from an intense desire to scratch yourself. Make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test to resist the urge. If you fail, receive a Fatigued Condition that is only removed if you spend your next 1d10 Actions scratching yourself.

When the Pox ends, attempt an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test. If this fails, reverse the Test dice and apply permanent scarring to that Hit Location, showing an area where you scratched and the pox there healed badly. If the Hit Location is the head, permanently lose -1 Fellowship. See page 164 to determine Hit Locations.

records.name: Treatment of Disease
records.text:
A character with at least one Advance in the Heal Skill may administer treatment to someone who has a disease. Each day the patient spends resting under their care, the duration of the disease is reduced by 1 additional day. A successful Challenging (+0 SL) Heal Test ensures that the carer does not contract the disease for that day, with each SL after the first extending this protection to one other character.

The GM may apply modifiers to this Heal Test to reflect the virulence of the disease, the suitability of conditions and materials, or the stress of your circumstances.

records.name: Dosage
records.text: Most poisons are prepared with the intention of harming a human-sized target. A dose of poison is defined as the amount needed to force a single Endurance Test on characters of Small or Average Size. For every additional dose applied, the Difficulty of the Endurance Test required to resist the poison worsens by 1 step. When used against creatures of different Sizes, more or less poison may be required.

records.name: Poisons
records.text:
Poisons can inflict some of the same symptoms as a disease, but the effects usually don’t last quite as long, and treating them requires identifying the poison and administering an appropriate antidote. A Difficult (-1 SL) Heal Test, or an Average (+2 SL) Trade (Poisoner) Test correctly identifies the poison and the antidote required, which could be anything from a herbal preparation to an alchemical concoction to something far more esoteric.

Poisoning is almost always handled by having the affected Character make an Endurance Test to avoid or mitigate the effects of the poison. The effects of poisons vary. Most commonly they impose Poisoned Conditions on the affected Character, but they may cause sleepiness, delirium, disease Symptoms, or a combination of such factors.

records.name: Psychology Test
records.text:
If you are exposed to one of the following Psychology Traits, you may resist its effects by passing a Psychology Test using the Cool Skill, with the Difficulty set by the GM. A successful Test lasts until the end of the current encounter, although additional Tests may be required if circumstances change.

Example: Brokk has Animosity (Elves). When the dwarf encounters some haughty elves sipping daintily from their wine glasses in a tavern, he must pass a Psychology Test to control himself. He rolls a 68, which is higher than his Cool of 40. Beard bristling, he stomps over to the elves and launches into a tirade about exactly what he thinks of their so-called nimbleness!

records.name: Conditions
records.text:
Conditions represent the effects of things that can happen to you in the course of your adventures. The Conditions you suffer from can be recorded on a scrap sheet of paper, or you can use chits or counters to represent them. Each Condition explains how long any effects usually last in its description; however, it is possible the cause of a Condition — such as a Spell or Critical Wound — may override this.

When you incur a Condition, you immediately lose Momentum. You can still gain Momentum while suffering from one, unless the Condition states otherwise.

mUlTiple CondiTions

You can be subject to the same Condition more than once; indeed, sometimes you will receive multiples of the same Condition from a single event. If this occurs, any penalties suffered are stacked. So, if you have 3 Bleeding Conditions, you are losing a worrying 3 Wounds per Round; or if you have 3 Fatigued Conditions, you suffer -3 SL to all Tests.

You can also be subject to multiple, different Conditions at once. When this occurs, the effects do not stack; you suffer the highest of the two penalties and apply it. So, if you had 1 Fatigued and the Prone Condition, you would suffer a -2 SL penalty to all active Tests, not -3 SL.

A Condition can be removed with a Fortune Point, so while they are debilitating, they can be managed if you are careful (see page 133).

records.name: Gaining Corruption Points
records.text:
Corruption Points are gained through exposure to places, people, or objects tainted by Chaos, or to situations especially favoured by the Dark Gods.

You do not Test for Corruption every time you are exposed. Instead, at the end of the session, the GM determines your greatest degree of exposure and calls for a single Corruption Test. Multiple exposures, or exposure to multiple sources, may increase the Test’s Difficulty, change the Characteristic Tested, or increase the Corruption gained on a failure, at the GM’s discretion. The stronger the Corrupting Influence, the more SL you must score to avoid gaining Corruption Points.

A Corruption Test is a Challenging (+0 SL) Endurance or Cool Test, as determined by the GM. Physical corruption is usually resisted with Endurance, while spiritual corruption is resisted with Cool. The stronger the Corrupting Influence, the more SL you must score to avoid gaining Corruption Points.

Note: Spellcasting, or having Spells cast on you, doesn’t cause Corruption unless explicitly stated. Simply using a Chaos Lore does not require you or allies to make Corruption Tests.

There are two types of exposure:

• Exposure: You have physical contact with the listed source for at least 1 Turn, or spend at least 1 hour in its vicinity or under its influence.

• Prolonged Exposure: You have physical contact with the listed source for at least 1 hour, or spend at least 6 hours in its vicinity or under its influence.

records.name: Minor Corruption
records.text:
These Corrupting Influences, although relatively trivial, still endanger a weak soul. If you fail a Test to resist Minor Corruption, gain 1 Corruption Point.

• Exposure to a creature with the Corruption (Minor) Trait, refined warpstone, or a profane artefact

• Prolonged Exposure to Chaos worshippers, Chaos cult temples, skaven, mutant lairs, and similar

records.name: Moderate Corruption
records.text:
Moderate Corrupting Influences are a danger to every soul and should be avoided under all circumstances. If you fail the Test, gain 2 Corruption Points. On a Marginal Success (+0 SL), gain 1 Corruption Point. On a Success (1+ SL), you gain no Corruption Points.

• Exposure to a creature with the Corruption (Moderate) Trait or warpstone

• Prolonged Exposure to refined warpstone or a Chaos- tainted artefact

records.name: Corrupting
records.text:
No one is left unscathed by exposure to the Ruinous Powers. Eventually, even the strongest fall, their mind and bodies twisting into new, unrecognisable forms.

Should you ever gain more Corruption Points than your Willpower Bonus plus your Toughness Bonus, immediately attempt a Challenging (+0 SL) Endurance Test. If passed, you have managed to hold off your corruption for now but will have to Test again next time you gain Corruption Points. If you fail, then either your body or mind is about to mutate.

records.name: Corruption Limits
records.text: A soul can withstand only so much corruption before it finally gives way. If you ever have more physical mutations than your Toughness Bonus, or more mental mutations than your Willpower Bonus, your soul is lost. Your Character has fallen to Chaos and it is time to create a new one. Your former Character becomes an NPC under the GM’s control, and you may yet encounter the wretched creature they have become…

records.name: Dissolution of Body and Mind
records.text:
As corruption ravages your soul, the warping breath of Chaos whispers within, either twisting your flesh into a fresh, new form, or fracturing your psyche with exquisite knowledge it can never unlearn.

First, lose Corruption Points equal to your Willpower Bonus as you mutate. Next, roll percentile dice and refer to the following table to determine whether it is your body or your mind that blossoms anew.

Next, roll on either the Physical Corruption Table or the Mental Corruption Table to see what happens.

records.name: Major Corruption
records.text:
Few mortals can withstand a Major Corrupting Influence for long. Remain in its presence, and Chaos will begin to reshape you. For each failed Major Corruption Test, gain 3 Corruption Points. If you succeed with a Marginal Success (+0 SL), gain 2 Corruption Points. On a Success (1–3 SL), you gain 1 Corruption Point. Only if you score an Impressive Success (4+ SL) do you gain no Corruption Points.

• Exposure to a creature with the Corruption (Major) Trait

• Prolonged Exposure to warpstone

• Making a deal with a daemon

• Consuming refined warpstone

records.name: Manifestation Time
records.text:
Mutations seldom manifest immediately. They may begin as an itch, a patch of flaky skin, or a nervous tic, only later developing into a wet and blinking extra eye, unexpected feathers, or a mind twisted beyond recognition. When you generate a mutation, the GM secretly rolls 3d10. The mutation manifests within that many days.

Use the descriptions in the tables to make your mutation uniquely horrifying. If it is obvious to others, you suffer significant penalties to Fellowship Tests as appropriate. More significantly, ordinary people will likely flee from your presence, the watch will be called, you will be pursued by witch hunters, and life will swiftly become very difficult.

records.name: Characteristic Advances
records.text:
Every Career has an Advance Scheme governing its Characteristic Advances. Three Characteristics are available at the first level of the Career. A further Characteristic becomes available at the second level (brass), third level (silver), and fourth level (gold).

The XP cost for Characteristic Advances is shown on the Advancement XP Costs table. Each Advance you purchase adds +5 to the associated Characteristic. The cost of purchasing Advances for a Characteristic increases depending on how many times you’ve already advanced that Characteristic.

Example: Your Initial Agility is 27 and you purchase your first Agility Advance. Your new Agility is 32. This costs you 125 XP. To increase your Agility by a further +5 to a total of 37 costs an additional 175 XP.

The cumulative XP cost is the cost required to increase a Characteristic if you have no prior Advances. For example, going from no Advances in Agility to +30 would cost 2,100 XP.

Note: While Weapon Skill and Ballistic Skill contain the word ‘Skill’, this is a historical artefact — they are Characteristics.

records.name: Purchasing Talents
records.text:
You can purchase any of the Talents listed for your current Career level as well as those from lower levels.

The rules for every Talent can be found in Chapter 4: Skills and Talents. Each Talent costs 100 XP, and purchasing it grants your Character access to the Talent’s special rules. Some Talents can be taken multiple times, for 100 XP each time, as listed in their description.

When you purchase a Talent from your Career, remember to tick one box on the Career Advancement Tracker.

records.name: Skill Advances
records.text:
You can advance all the Skills listed for your Career level and lower. The cost in XP of a Skill Advance is shown in the Advancement XP Costs table, and depends on the number of Skill Advances you have already taken in that Skill.

Each Skill Advance adds +5 to your Skill level. XP Costs for Skills increase in the same way as for Characteristics.

Example: You purchase your first Advance (+5) in Stealth and your Agility was 31, your Stealth would be 36. This costs 50 XP. Increasing this by a further +5 to 41 would cost an additional 75 XP. The full rules for how to use your Skills can be found in Chapter 4: Skills and Talents. Like Characteristic Advances, there is no upper limit to the number of Skill Advances that can be purchased. The table below presents costs for even the most ambitious campaigns and improbably successful characters.

records.name: Spending XP
records.text:
Between adventures, you may spend XP to advance your Characteristics and Skills, acquire new Talents, and advance your Career Level. Your Career Level determines what Characteristics, Skills, and Talents are available to you.

You can also use XP to change Career, see the Change Career Endeavour, page 197.

records.name: Blessings and Miracles
records.text: Blessing and Miracles are prayers spoken by one of the Blessed, and then empowered by a god. To enact a Blessing or Miracle, make a Challenging (+0 SL) Pray Test. If you score a success, your Blessing or Miracle manifests according to its rules, and a high SL will give you bonus effects. If you score a failure, your words are spoken, but your god, for whatever reason, refuses to listen. If you Fumble the Pray Test, you have offended your god and must roll on the Wrath of the Gods table.

records.name: Limitations
records.text:
You must be able to speak to intone the required prayer, rite, chant, or song to enact a Blessing or Miracle. Each of your Blessings or Miracles can only be in effect once, meaning you have to wait for an existing one to come to an end before using the same prayer again. Each of the gods have different styles of prayers, designed to be intoned in different ways. Whether these are the warcries of Ulric, the shanties of Manann, or the threnodies of Morr, each requires the words be spoken (or sung) firmly, and with conviction.

To represent this, the GM may require that any Pray Tests that are intoned quietly or without confidence have a higher Difficulty.

Multiple invocations of the same prayer by different individuals do not offer cumulative bonuses. Thus, intoning two Blessings of Finesse will only provide a bonus of +10 to Dexterity.

records.name: Sin Points
records.text:
The Blessed are watched closely by the gods, and risk gaining the disfavour of their deities if they should act contrary to their gods’ will. In game, this is represented with Sin Points.

If you violate any of the cult strictures listed under your god, the GM will award one or more Sin Points depending on the severity of your offence. Every time you receive a Sin Point, it is added to your running total. There is no maximum to the number of Sin Points you can earn. The more points you have, the more upset your god is likely to be should you call upon divine aid.

records.name: The Blessed
records.text: There are two Talents that specifically mark out those Blessed by the gods: Bless and Invoke. Characters with the Bless Talent may enact Blessings, which are minor manifestations of divine will, while the Invoke Talent allows the Blessed to call on their gods for more powerful Miracles. For more on these Talents, see Chapter 4: Skills and Talents.

records.name: Sin and Wrath
records.text: Appealing to your deity when you have been acting contrary to the god’s wishes is risky. Whenever you make a Pray Test, if the units die of the result is equal to or less than your current Sin Point total, then you will suffer the Wrath of the Gods, even if the Pray Test is successful.

records.name: Wrath of the Gods
records.text:
Whenever you Fumble a Pray Test, or when the units die of a Pray Test is equal or lower than your current Sin Points, roll on the Wrath of the Gods table. The GM may also use it, or pluck results from it, whenever you foolishly insult any of the gods.

When rolling on the Wrath of the Gods table, add +10 to the roll for each Sin Point you have accrued. After rolling and applying the result, reduce your Sin points by 1, to a minimum of 0.

records.name: Absolution
records.text: If a character behaves in a particularly pious manner, such as completing an arduous pilgrimage, or making a significant donation to their cult, the GM may wish to remove one or more Sin Points with a successful Pray Test, used to show you are begging for absolution. This, of course, also risks the chance of Wrath of the Gods. Otherwise, the only way to remove Sin Points is by rolling on the Wrath of the Gods table.

records.name: Penance
records.text:
Some Wrath of the Gods results require penance. The GM can decide upon a suitable penance depending on your misdeed, or they may prefer you to choose your own penance, with further punishment awaiting if you are insufficiently penitent. Examples of typical penances are listed in each cult description. Penances may come in the form of a vision, divine inspiration or, very rarely, by direct communication from your deity. If you are not worthy of such contact, a penance may be conveyed through another member of your cult. Alternatively, a Divine Servant of the cult could manifest — this could be a dead teacher, a figure of legend, or an appropriate animal — and inform you what is required. records.name: Casting Test
records.text:
You can cast Spells you have memorised or those you can read from a grimoire (see page 237). To cast a Spell, make a Challenging (+0 SL) Language (Magick) Test.

If the Casting Test is successful, calculate the SL and compare it to the CN of the Spell. If the SL is equal to or greater than the CN, you cast the Spell as explained in the Spell description. If not, the Spell fails.

records.name: Critical Casting
records.text:
If you roll doubles on a successful Casting Test, you cause a Critical Casting. Roll on the Minor Miscast Table (page 238). Note that the Instinctive Diction Talent may help mitigate the risk of Miscasts. If you Critically Cast, you may choose one of the three extra effects:

•  Critical Damage: If the Spell causes Damage, it also inflicts a Critical Wound to the Hit Location struck (or the Body if none is defined).

•  Total Power: The Spell is cast. You may add the tens digit of your Casting Test to your SL for the purpose of Overcasting.

•  Unstoppable Force: The Spell may not be dispelled (see page 237).

Petty Spells do not cause Critical Casting or a Minor Miscast on a Critical.

records.name: Duration
records.text: A successfully cast Spell lasts for its Duration. If you wish for a Spell to last for a shorter time than it normally would, you must declare how long the Spell will remain in effect when the Spell is cast. Once the Spell is in effect, it can only be ended before the duration elapses by dispelling it.

records.name: Fumbled Casting
records.text: If you roll doubles on a failed Casting Test, you Fumble the cast. Roll on the Minor Miscast Table.

records.name: Ingredients
records.text:
You may channel your magic through an appropriate ingredient before unleashing your Spell. This protects against Miscasts as the attuned ingredient absorbs the worst of any magical backlash.

To use an ingredient while casting, declare that you are doing so before making the Casting Test. Ingredients reduce Miscast level by one step: reducing a Major Miscast to a Minor one, or reducing a Minor Miscast to no effect.

The ingredient is consumed by the process, even if no Miscast was rolled. Ingredients must be bought for a single Spell and normally cost half the Spell’s CN in silver shillings.

records.name: Magic Missiles
records.text: Magic missiles are damage-causing Spells. When a magic missile is successfully cast, reverse the dice on the Casting Test to determine where the target is struck using the Hit Locations table (page 164). To calculate Damage, add your Willpower Bonus to the Spell’s listed Damage. This Damage is reduced by the target’s Toughness Bonus and Armour Points as usual.

records.name: Spellcasting Limitations
records.text:
You must speak or sing to cast Spells. If your voice is inhibited, the GM should increase the Difficulty of Casting Tests by one step.

When Spells provide bonuses or impose penalties, the best bonus and worst penalty is applied from all Spells that affect the target. They do not stack.

Unless otherwise stated, you must have line of sight to your target.

records.name: Touch Spells in Combat
records.text:
Certain Spells require you to touch the target. To touch a creature who does not wish to be touched, make an Opposed Melee (Brawling) or Sleight of Hand Test (generally Opposed by the target’s Dodge or Melee Skill) after making a successful Casting Test. If the Spell is a magic missile, reverse the Touch Test to determine the Hit Location struck.

Certain magical items, such as enchanted staffs, allow you to benefit from their reach when casting touch Spells. In this case, you may replace Melee (Brawling) or Sleight of Hand with an appropriate Melee Skill, such as Melee (Polearm) in the case of an enchanted staff. This Test is made purely to see if you touch the target with the item. It is not a separate attack that would inflict Damage in addition to the effects of the Spell.

records.name: Channelling
records.text:
You can gather the magical energy needed to cast powerful Spells by channelling. To channel magic, you must decide which Wind of Magic you wish to channel and use your Action to make a Challenging (+0 SL) Channelling Test.

Each SL gathered through channelling adds to a pool of power. When you make a Casting Test for a spell of the appropriate Lore, you may add the SL gathered through channelling to the SL of your Casting Test. After making a Casting Test, all gathered power is lost. If you stop Channelling for any reason, you may make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test — if you fail, the power is lost.

records.name: Critical and Fumbled Channelling
records.text:
Rolling a double on a successful Channelling Test adds an additional Willpower Bonus SL to your pool of power. If you fail and roll doubles, lose 1d10 SL and then roll on the Minor Miscast Table, adding +10 to the result for each SL of power lost.

If you take damage or suffer a Condition while channelling, you must make a Hard (-2 SL) Cool Test or lose 1d10 SL and roll on the Minor Miscast table, adding +10 per SL as above.

records.name: Overcasting
records.text:
If a Casting Test generates SL beyond those required to cast a spell, you can spend the remaining SL on Overcasting. You can spend a number of SL equal to your Intelligence Bonus plus Willpower Bonus in this way.

•  Overcasting can add additional Range, Area of Effect, Duration, or Targets to the Spell. If the Spell is a magic missile, it can also add to the Damage. Spells may have additional options in their descriptions.

•  Spells with a Range of ‘You’ only ever target the spellcaster. Spells with a range of ‘Touch’ or a duration of ‘Instant’ or ‘Special’ may not be extended. Spells with no Area of Effect may not have their area increased.

•  Petty Spells cannot be Overcast.
