records.name: Second Sight
records.text: The Second Sight Talent allows you to perceive the Winds of Magic, and may use it to aid you in Perception, Track, or other Skill Tests where traces of the Winds of Magic might provide clues. A Character with the Second Sight Talent cannot simply turn it off, even should they wish to. In areas truly saturated by the Winds of Magic, they suffer Disadvantage on Perception Tests to perceive mundane phenomena.

records.name: Armour Repels the Winds
records.text:
Metal and leather armour can make it harder for a spellcaster to control magical energy due to the fact that they attract Chamon (in the case of metal) or Ghur (in the case of leather). Spellcasters wearing armour suffer -1 SL to all Casting and Channelling Tests for every Armour Point on the Location with the most armour. Casters using Chamon may wear metal armour without penalty, and those using Ghur may wear leather armour without penalty. Armour Points granted by Spells do not repel the Spell’s Wind.

When creating a creature with the Spellcaster Trait or using a Magician Template (see Chapter 12: Bestiary), they typically eschew armour in order to make the most of their magical powers. Chaos sorcerers may wear Chaos Armour without penalty. Creatures granted an Armour Trait by their own scales or hide do not suffer penalties.

records.name: Dispelling
records.text: Once per Round, you may attempt to dispel any Spell that targets a creature or point you can see within Willpower yards. Make an Opposed Language (Magick) Test against the spellcaster attempting to cast the Spell. If you win, the Spell is dispelled and has no effect. If the casting spellcaster wins the Opposed Test, use the SL for the Casting Test.

records.name: Dispelling Persistent Spells
records.text:
You may attempt to dispel a Spell with a lasting effect as an Action. Make an Extended Challenging (+0 SL) Language (Magick) Test. When your SL reaches the CN of the ongoing Spell, it is dispelled.

Multiple spellcasters attempting to dispel the same Spell make Tests separately. If they know the same Lore of Magic, then they can provide Assistance instead. A spellcaster dispelling their own Spell receives +1 SL to the Language (Magick) Test.

records.name: Grimoires
records.text:
Grimoires are books containing instructions on how to cast Spells. A typical grimoire contains notes of four Spells from the same Lore of Magic.

You may cast a Spell from a grimoire if the Spell belongs to a Lore of Magic that you possess. You need both hands free to flick through the pages. You cannot Overcast an unmemorised Spell; you need familiarity to modify it beyond the basics.

records.name: Malignant Influences
records.text:
If you are subject to a Corrupting Influence and make a Casting Test or Channelling Test, there is an additional risk. Any time you would normally roll on the Minor Miscast Table, you must roll on the Major Miscast Table instead.

Spellcasters do not count as Malignant Influences in regard to their own Casting and Channelling Tests.

records.name: Memorising Spells
records.text: You can memorise Spells by spending the amount of XP noted in the Petty Magic, Arcane Magic, and Chaos Magic Talents.

records.name: Multiple Arcane Lores
records.text: An elf spellcaster may learn a number of Arcane Lores equal to their Willpower Bonus. An elf Character may not purchase a new Arcane Magic Talent until they have learned at least 8 Spells from the previous Lore. Any spellcaster may learn a

records.name: Using Warpstone
records.text:
Some spellcasters prize warpstone as it can be used as a magical fuel. If you have a piece of warpstone, double any SL you generate on Casting Tests or Channelling Tests. Warpstone counts as a Malignant Influence as explained above.

When warpstone is used as a magical fuel, it is gradually consumed. Keep track of how many CN a particular piece of warpstone has provided. One gram of warpstone is consumed for every 20 CN of magical energy it provides.

In the Empire, the cults and various secular authorities take an extremely dim view of the use of warpstone, and those who possess or use it will be considered to be undertaking acts of Witchcraft even if they are licensed by a College of Magic. There is a thriving black market for the stuff if you possess the right contacts, though it is expensive. While all spellcasters might benefit from warpstone, skaven spellcasters use it as the primary source of their magical power. All Casting Tests and Channelling Tests made by skaven suffer from -4 SL unless they possess a piece of warpstone. The most accomplished skaven grey seers are experts in utilising warpstone, and do not count it as a Malignant Influence, though other skaven spellcasters do.

records.name: Coin and Status
records.text:
Characters of a given Status most frequently use the coinage associated with their status.

•  Brass Tier: The poorest members of society are unlikely to see a gold coin in their lifetimes. They live humble lives, subsisting on plain foods and sleeping in shared rooms.

•  Silver Tier: The swelling middle classes may use pennies for ale and gold for major purchases, but shillings are their standard currency.

•  Gold Tier: The wealthiest elites rarely bother themselves with pennies, occasionally use silver to pay their underlings, and often enjoy the awe producing a gold coin can inspire in their social inferiors.

For GMs preferring hard numbers, spending around half your Status every day is usually enough to maintain appearances, though you may be living a little frugally. So, if you have a Status of Silver 4, spending at least 2 shillings per day will do for food and board, where if you have Brass 2 Status, you need only spend a pfennig a day.

records.name: Money
records.text:
The Empire’s coins are usually minted in three denominations: brass pennies (d), silver shillings (/), and gold crowns (GC). Coins weigh around an ounce and, as their inherent value is determined by weight, even foreign coins can be easily valued with a set of scales, though they will likely draw a suspicious eye.

Standard coin values are: 1 gold crown (1 GC) = 20 silver shillings (20/–) = 240 brass pennies (240d) 1 silver shilling (1/–) = 12 brass pennies (12d) This is usually abbreviated to: 1 GC = 20/– = 240d

records.name: Availability
records.text:
All Trappings have an Availability: either Common, Scarce, Rare, or Exotic.

Common items are found in almost every corner of the Empire and are always assumed to be readily available.

Scarce and Rare items are less common, and you need to pass an Availability Test to find any locally in stock; the chance of passing the Test depends upon the settlement size.

Exotic items are exceedingly rare, and only available if the GM says so, or if you commission the item from an appropriate artisan (perhaps with a Commission Endeavour, see page 197), or make it yourself (perhaps with a Crafting Endeavour, see page 198).

Once you know an item’s Availability, check it on the following table to see if it is in stock.

| Availability | Village | Town | City |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Common | In stock! | In stock! | In stock! |
| Scarce | 30% | 60% | 90% |
| Rare | 15% | 30% | 45% |
| Exotic | Not in stock | Not in stock | Not in stock |

If you fail an Availability Test for Scarce or Rare items, you can either reroll when you arrive at a new settlement or you can try again next week if the settlement is Town-size or larger.

• The GM may overrule Availability as dictated by local details. For example, basic rowboats are automatically available if the adventure is located in a fishing village that features a renowned boat-builder.

• Availability percentages can be increased by +10% or +20% if you are especially diligent, belong to a relevant Career such as Merchant or Fence, or spend an entire day shopping and making Gossip Tests.

records.name: Clipping
records.text: Embezzlers can trim slivers of precious metal away from the edges of coins. This scam is called ‘clipping’ or ‘shaving’ and is practised mainly by shopkeepers or tollkeepers who have access to large quantities of other peoples’ money. Gold and silver filings are then melted down and sold to jewellers, counterfeiters, or fences. Clipped coins can be detected with the Evaluate Skill; the more clipped the coin, the easier the Test.

records.name: Counterfeiting
records.text:
The diversity of coinage circulating the Empire means counterfeiting is rife. Reiklanders may be accustomed to seeing coins from other provinces, but are always wary of being scammed.

A successful Evaluate Test will detect counterfeit coins, typically by inspecting coins for weight and hardness.

Actually producing counterfeit coins is much harder. It requires an Art (Engraving) Test to carve a convincing stamping die, then a Trade (Smith) Test to strike the coins, usually with the aid of an assistant. Including a higher precious metal content makes Evaluate Tests to detect counterfeits more difficult; using less than a fifth makes it much easier to spot the fake coins.

records.name: Going to Market
records.text: Once you start play, the availability of rarer goods is restricted. A village market may only have a few locally sourced goods for sale, whilst the emporiums and market squares of the Empire’s cities may contain all manner of exotic fare.

records.name: Bargaining and Trading
records.text:
People of the Empire love a good bargain, and eager shoppers fill town squares looking for the best deals. When buying goods, there are two primary Skills to Test: Evaluate and Haggle.

Evaluate is used to identify the quality of an item (see Craftsmanship below). Vendors can use Evaluate to appraise coins for their exchange value, or spot counterfeits. Anyone can also use Evaluate to estimate the prices of Rare or Exotic items.

Haggle is used by buyers and sellers, typically in Opposed Tests. Haggling is expected and most prices are marked up to account for this. See page 143 for the effects of using the Haggle Skill.

records.name: Bartering
records.text: Rural and mercantile commerce often involves trading one commodity for another without exchanging money. Some folks see this as a preferable and more honest form of exchange that does away with the risk of fraudulent currency and unwelcome taxation. If you wish to barter one or more items for something of roughly equivalent value, note the Availability of the rarest item involved in the transaction. Halve this value, rounding down, and roll to see if you’ve found someone wiling to partake in the trade. If successful, the deal goes ahead, though players may make a Haggle Test if they want to argue for more favourable terms. It is up to the GM if anyone is willing to make a particular trade — looted hand weapons may be of limited use to a boat builder, for example.

records.name: Craftsmanship
records.text:
The items available in the shops, stalls, and merchant halls of the Empire vary significantly in quality. Not everything is made equal, and the Craftsmanship rules reflect this using Item Qualities and Item Flaws.

An Item Quality makes the trapping a little better, but harder to find. An Item Flaw makes the trapping a little worse, but easier to find.

records.name: Item Qualities
records.text: A Trapping is called a Quality Trapping if it has more Item Qualities than Flaws.

records.name: Lowering the Price
records.text:
If you cannot find a buyer, you can try lowering the price. Each time you halve the money you are willing to accept, the Availability of a buyer increases by one step.

Example: Corporal Schütze has fled his State Army regiment with a stolen Hochland Long Rifle, and is keen to sell. As it is an Exotic item, there are no immediate buyers he can find on the street. The GM determines the base price Schütze can expect is half the weapon’s value (so 50 GC), so Schütze decides to drop the price by half two times, saying he will accept 12 GC 10/–, which increases the Availability of a buyer two steps from Exotic to Scarce.

records.name: Selling
records.text:
Selling your Trappings during desperate times, or simply offloading loot, is handled in exactly the same fashion as buying, but this time you will be making money, not spending it. So, you first check for Availability of a buyer in the same fashion as checking for stock. You then bargain and trade, with Evaluate Tests and Haggle Tests as the GM prefers, and finally you set a price. Typically, the base cost when selling is half the item’s listed price, meaning, when selling second-hand, you usually make between a quarter to half an item’s worth after Haggling.

If you put time into Gossip Tests and wandering the local town, you might find someone willing to pay up to 80% of the item’s listed value, though that is left in the hands of the GM.

records.name: Beasts of Burden
records.text: Encumbrance Points for draft animals and vehicles like mules, horses, carts, and wagons are listed in their descriptions. Each human-sized passenger is assumed to weigh around 10 Encumbrance Points, modified by the GM as necessary.

records.name: Encumbrance
records.text:
Even the doughtiest Dwarf cannot carry a limitless number of Trappings. To help you track how much you are carrying, all items are marked as weighing a number of Encumbrance Points (sometimes abbreviated to ‘Enc’), typically from 0–3, where 0 shows a trifling item that is easily carried, and 3 represents something that is a struggle to heft. The number of Encumbrance Points you can carry without penalty is determined by your Strength Bonus + Toughness Bonus. Thus, average Humans begin play able to carry around 6 Encumbrance Points.

### Encumbrance Examples

| Enc | Example Trappings |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Knives, coins, jewellery |
| 1 | Sword, mandolin, sling bag |
| 2 | Bastard sword, tent, backpack |
| 3 | Halberd, cask, large sack |

### Small Items

Common sense usually dictates the number of smaller items someone can carry before becoming Encumbered. To provide a rough guide, money weighs 1 Encumbrance Point per 200 coins.

### Oversized Items

Certain large items weigh 4 or more Encumbrance Points, such as barrels or saddlebags. You may normally only carry one oversized object, and it likely requires both hands.

### Beasts of Burden

Encumbrance Points for draft animals and vehicles like mules, horses, carts, and wagons are listed in their descriptions. Each human-sized passenger is assumed to weigh around 10 Encumbrance Points, modified by the GM as necessary.

### Worn Items

Worn items like armour and clothing have their Encumbrance reduced by 1, often counting as Encumbrance 0 when worn.

### Overburdened

Characters who exceed their Encumbrance capacity are slowed and prone to fatigue. Movement reduction and Travel Fatigue incurred from Encumbrance stacks with any Armour penalties. Endurance Tests to resist the Fatigued Condition incur Disadvantage while Overburdened.

### Overburdened Examples

| Enc | Penalty |
| --- | --- |
| Up to limit | No penalties |
| Up to double limit | −1 Movement (min. 3), −10 Agility, +1 Travel Fatigue |
| Up to triple limit | −2 Movement (min. 2), −20 Agility (min. 10), +2 Travel Fatigue |
| More than 3× | You are unable to move |

### Encumbrance and Attributes

Movement and Agility penalties for Encumbrance are applied immediately and can only be removed by dropping equipment.

### Encumbrance and Travel Fatigue

Fatigued Conditions are accrued at the end of a day’s travel and can only be removed with a long rest.

records.name: Item Flaws
records.text:
A Trapping is called a Flawed Trapping if it has more Item Flaws than Qualities. Each Flaw halves the listed price and improves Availability by one step. Many vendors sell Flawed items, but pretend they are anything but. A successful Test with any appropriate Skill — such as Evaluate, or Melee for weapons, or Trade for tools — will spot such underhanded activities.

Note: Exotic items do not have their Availability modified by being Flawed — they are always difficult to find, even shoddy examples.

Example: A suit of plate armour that is both Bulky and Unreliable costs a quarter of the list price, and raises Availability from Rare to Common.

records.name: Cavalry
records.text: Cavalry weapons are assumed to be used when mounted. When on foot, all two-handed weapons in the Cavalry Weapon Group also count as Two-handed weapons. Single-handed Cavalry weapons count as Improved Weapons when unmounted unless otherwise stated.

records.name: Fencing
records.text: Those with Melee (Basic) can use Fencing weapons, but cannot use their Weapon Qualities.

records.name: Flail
records.text: Unskilled Characters add the Dangerous Weapon Flaw.

records.name: Melee Weapon Groups
records.text: All melee weapons are assigned to a Weapon Group. Each Weapon Group requires a separate Skill to master its use. So, Melee (Flail) allows you to use Flails and is a separate Skill from Melee (Polearm), which allows you to use Polearms. If you use a weapon from a Group where you have no Advances, you Test your Weapon Skill to hit with the weapon. While you still suffer all the weapon’s Flaws, you cannot use any of its Qualities. Some Melee Weapon Groups also have special rules.

records.name: Weapon Reach
records.text:
The lengths of the weapons are progressively bigger as follows.

•  Personal: Your legs and fists, perhaps your head, and anything attached to those

•  Very Short: Less than a foot in length

•  Short: Up to 2 feet in length

•  Average: Up to 3 feet long

•  Long: Up to 6 foot long

•  Very Long: Up to 10 feet in length; can Engage enemies up to 4 yards away, rather than just 2

•  Massive: Anything over 10 feet long; can Engage enemies up to 6 yards away, rather than just 2

records.name: Weapon Reach and Defence
records.text: If your weapon is longer than your opponent’s, you benefit from +1 SL to defensive Melee Tests as you find it easier to keep them at bay.

records.name: Blackpowder and Explosives
records.text: Those with Ranged (Engineering) can use Blackpowder and Explosive weapons without penalty.

records.name: Crossbows and Throwing
records.text: Crossbows and Throwing weapons are relatively simple to use. You can use Crossbow and Throwing weapons with Ballistic Skill, but Ballistic Skill Tests suffer from –1 SL.

records.name: Engineering
records.text: You can use all Engineering weapons with Ranged (Blackpowder), but Ranged (Blackpowder) Tests suffer from a penalty of –2 SL.

records.name: Ranged Weapon Groups
records.text:
Ranged weapons are difficult to master. You cannot attempt a Ranged Test for a weapon you do not have the correct speciality for.

So, if you know Ranged (Blackpowder), you cannot attempt a Ranged (Bow) Test. However, there are a few exceptions.

records.name: Weapon Range
records.text:
A weapon’s range is its Medium range in yards. Chapter 5: Rules presents modifiers if a weapon is at Point Blank, Short, Long, or Extreme range. Calculate ranges as follows:

### Calculating Range Bands

| Band | Range |
| --- | --- |
| Point Blank | 4 yards |
| Short | Range ÷ 2 |
| Medium | Listed weapon range |
| Long | Range × 2 |
| Extreme | Range × 3 |

### Example Weapon Ranges

| Weapon | Point Blank | Short | Medium | Long | Extreme |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bow | 4 | 25 | 50 | 100 | 150 |
| Hochland Long Rifle | 4 | 50 | 100 | 200 | 300 |
| Pistol | 4 | 10 | 20 | 40 | 60 |
| Sling | 4 | 20 | 40 | 80 | 120 |

records.name: Armour
records.text:
‘Straps tight! A secure helm is the difference between the armourers fixing a dent and me having to find some poor sod to replace you.’ – Sergeant Hubrecht Grünner, Schilderheim Militia Leader

Armour is listed in the following format:

•  Armour Type: Each armour is listed by type.

•  Price: The price to buy an average piece of the armour.

•  Enc: The Encumbrance for the armour.

•  Availability: The Availability of the armour.

•  Penalty: Any penalty for wearing that specific piece of Armour in addition to those opposed by Encumbrance (page 299). Note: Some armour brings a penalty if you wear any of it, such as wearing any chain brings a penalty of –1 SL to Stealth Tests.

•  Locations: The Hit Locations the Armour protects.

•  AP: The number of Armour Points the armour provides to the protected Hit Locations.

•  Qualities and Flaws: Any Armour Qualities or Flaws the armour may possess.

records.name: Armour and Size
records.text: Armour gets heavier and more expensive the larger the creature it is made for. For each step above Size (Average), a piece of armour gains +1 Encumbrance and doubles in price. Conversely, for each step below Size (Average), subtract –1 Encumbrance and halve the price.

records.name: Creatures and Equipment
records.text:
Melee weapons are listed in a creature’s attacks showing the weapon’s name, its Skill with that weapon and the total Damage it inflicts (the creature’s Strength Bonus is included) in parentheses, followed by any Qualities or Flaws in italics. For example, a spear-armed creature would have: Spear (30/+7) Impale.

Ranged weapons are listed with the weapon and ammunition it uses, followed by parentheses containing the creature’s Skill with that weapon and the total Damage it inflicts (appropriate Strength Bonus is included), its range in yards, and any Qualities or Flaws in italics. For example, a creature armed with a Bow and Arrows would have: Bow and Arrows (30/+7) 50 yards, Impale.

Many creatures are armed with teeth, claws, horns, or other natural weaponry as their primary weapon. Unless otherwise mentioned, the Reach of such weapons is Personal and they possess no Qualities or Flaws.

Where an Armour value is provided, the total Toughness Bonus + Armour Points is shown in parentheses.

Armour and Weapons given to bipedal creatures with hands are just suggestions. If the GM wishes, such creatures could be armed and armoured with anything from the Consumer Guide, and can be assumed to have any Skills they need to use the items without penalty.

records.name: Customising Creatures
records.text:
The information presented is for the basic example of each particular individual. You can adapt these entries for variety, or to create more powerful creatures, by changing their Characteristics and adding Skills, Talents, and Creature Traits. The quickest way to create fast NPC adversaries is to use Creature Traits; all creatures come with one or more Creature Traits as standard, but additional ones can be added as required. The listed Optional Traits for a creature present common variants of the species, but you can apply any Trait to any creature if it fits your game. See page 356 for Creature Traits.

The templates on page 353 are a quick way of creating a variety of opponents from more organised species or societies. Apply the template to the basic information for the species to create a Soldier, Skirmisher, Elite, Leader, Commander, Spellcaster, or Spellcaster Lord. You could even use the Career system to develop well rounded and, depending on how much XP you decide to spend on them, terrifyingly powerful allies or antagonists.

records.name: Individual Characteristic Advances
records.text:
Characteristic and Skill Advances are bought in +5 increments. However, in some cases, a player might want to purchase individual Advances. This might be because they just need a point or two to get to a Characteristic to a round number and thus increase their Characteristic Bonus, or because they prefer frequent modest improvements over larger jumps in ability.

Use the table below to determine the XP cost for individual Advances. Once you switch to this method, you need to have bought a number Advances that is a multiple of 5 if you wish to return to the method presented on page 191.

| Advances | Characteristic: cost per +1 | Skills: cost per +1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 to 5 | 25 | 10 |
| 6 to 10 | 35 | 15 |
| 11 to 15 | 50 | 20 |
| 16 to 20 | 70 | 30 |
| 21 to 25 | 100 | 50 |
| 26 to 30 | 140 | 80 |
| 31 to 35 | 190 | 120 |
| 36 to 40 | 260 | 170 |
| 41 to 45 | 360 | 170 |
| 46 to 50 | 510 | 340 |
| 51 to 55 | 720 | 500 |
| 56 to 60 | 1005 | 700 |
| 61 to 65 | 1390 | 950 |
| 66 to 70 | 1800 | 1300 |
| 71+ | 2250 | 1700 |

records.name: Animal Care
records.text: Care for animals and heal them from disease or injury. A Character with an Advance in this Skill can keep animals healthy under normal conditions without needing to Test. A Test is required to diagnose or resolve problems with animals, such as spotting signs of illness or healing an injury (page 171).

records.name: Animal Training
records.text: Specialisations: Demigryph, Dog, Hawk, Horse, Pigeon Your understanding of a particular type of animal, and ability to train them. To train a beast, undertake the Animal Training Endeavour between adventures (see page 196).

records.name: Art
records.text: Specialisations: Drawing, Engraving, Mosaics, Painting, Sculpture, Tattooing, Weaving, Writing. Create works of art in your chosen medium. The more SL achieved, the better the quality of the final piece. For complicated or large works of art, an Extended Test may be required.

records.name: Athletics
records.text: Your ability to run, jump, move or perform any other general physical activity.

records.name: Bribery
records.text: Find someone who is willing to accept a bribe, such as a guild notary to accept forged paperwork or a gate guard to look the other way while you slip inside after nightfall. You can also make a Bribery Test to judge if a particular person could be bribed, and what their price is likely to be.

records.name: Channelling
records.text: Specialisations Include: Aqshy, Azyr, Chamon, Dhar, Ghur, Ghyran, Hysh, Magick, Shyish, Ulgu. Ability to call upon and control the various Winds of Magic, solely used with the magic rules. See Chapter 8: Magic for details.

records.name: Charm
records.text: Makes people think favourably of you, your opinions, and actions you propose. People won’t necessarily do what you say simply because you’ve passed a Charm Test, but they will at least give you due consideration.

records.name: Charm Animal
records.text: Your aptitude for befriending, quickly calming, or subjugating animals. A Charm Animal Test can convince a wild animal to back off, or a guard dog to devour a proffered scrap of meat rather than your arm.

records.name: Climb
records.text: The ability to ascend steep or vertical surfaces, like a perilous mountainside or the rain-slick wall of a tumbledown townhouse. Climbing can sometimes be used in combat when facing especially monstrous foes — see page 162 for combat movement.

records.name: Consume Alcohol
records.text: How well you can handle alcohol without letting it cloud your judgment or render you senseless. Often used to impress those who find the ability to down an unreasonable number of beverages to be praiseworthy.

records.name: Cool
records.text: Allows you to remain calm under stress, resist fear in the face of horror, and stick to your convictions. It is generally used to resist the attempts of others to Charm or Intimidate you, or to curtail other Psychological effects (see page 183).

records.name: Dodge
records.text: Avoid things through ducking, diving, and moving quickly, and is used extensively to sidestep falling rocks, incoming weapons, and the like. In combat, Dodge is generally used to resist attacks or avoid damage.

records.name: Drive
records.text: Maneuvering vehicles — most commonly simple carts and lumbering coaches, but also the more experimental creations of Imperial Engineers — along the roads of the Empire with as little incident as possible.

records.name: Endurance
records.text: Called upon when you must endure hardship, withstand deprivation, stand without moving for long periods of time, or survive harsh environments. In particular, Endurance is Tested to resist or recover from various Conditions (see page 184) and helps you recover lost Wounds (see page 170).

records.name: Entertain
records.text: Specialisations: Acting, Comedy, Singing, Storytelling. Delight crowds with the spoken word, perhaps by singing, acting, or attempting a few jokes — hopefully entertaining all those within earshot.

records.name: Evaluate
records.text: Lets you determine the value of goods. Everybody is assumed to know the relative worth of general items, but Evaluate allows you to identify the value of curious and unique items, recognise forgeries, or spot flaws.

records.name: Gamble
records.text: Measure the likelihood that a bet will pay off, as well as successfully engage in various games of chance. If you wish to improve your chances through cheating, see page 135.

records.name: Gossip
records.text: Ferret out interesting and useful news, and spread rumours of your own. Best practised at a town square, inn, well, or other gathering place.

records.name: Haggle
records.text: Secure better deals when negotiating with others, when purchasing goods for example. Typically involves an Opposed Haggle Test (page 131).

records.name: Heal
records.text: You have been trained to deal with injuries and diseases. A successful Heal Test allows you to diagnose illness, treat a disease, heal wounds or staunch a Bleeding Condition. Full rules for illness, injury, and treatments can be found on page 172.

records.name: Intimidate
records.text: Coerce or frighten sentient creatures — generally with an overt threat, though sometimes a subtle implication or even a look is enough.

records.name: Intuition
records.text: Gives you a feel for your surroundings, to notice when something is wrong, and read people to sense when they are lying or hiding something.

records.name: Language
records.text: Specialisations: Bretonnian, Reikspiel, Wastelander, and many more. See page 149. Access to extra languages beyond your native tongue. A single Advance is enough to make yourself understood in that language, but a Test may be required to comprehend complicated discussions. Once you have 4 Advances, you count as fluent and no longer need to make Tests.

records.name: Leadership
records.text: Your ability to lead others and command respect. While most often associated with martial situations, a resolute leader can quickly direct a fast response to a fire or other such calamity, and nobles use the Skill frequently to command their lessers.

records.name: Lore
records.text: Specialisations: Engineering, Geology, Heraldry, History, Law, Local*, Magic, Metallurgy, Science, Theology. Knowledge of a subject you have been taught or have first-hand knowledge of. Basic facts related to a specific Lore Skill can be recalled easily, with a Test required only to recall obscure or unusual information.

records.name: Melee
records.text: Specialisations: Basic, Brawling, Cavalry, Fencing, Flail, Parry, Polearm, Two-handed. Training and experience with a single type of close combat weaponry. Each Melee Specialisation indicates expertise in using a specific class of weapon. If you do not have the correct Specialisation for a weapon, you will usually suffer a penalty when using it — see Chapter 11: Consumer Guide for more.

records.name: Navigation
records.text: Allows you to find your way in the wilderness, or across the ocean, using landmarks, stellar bodies, charts, or maps.

records.name: Outdoor Survival
records.text: Used to survive in the wild, including the ability to fish, hunt, forage, and build fires and shelters. Experienced survivors are practiced at reading the signs of incoming inclement weather, making do with minimal tools, and noticing the spoor of local beasts.

records.name: Perception
records.text: Your ability to notice things with your senses — sight, smell, hearing, touch, taste, and any other senses you may possess, such as magical or inhuman senses.

records.name: Perform
records.text: Specialisations: Acrobatics, Clowning, Dancing, Firebreathing, Juggling, Miming, Rope Walking. You have learned a physically demanding art, perhaps as a way to make a living. A successful Perform Test lets you entertain those near enough to see you.

records.name: Pick Lock
records.text: You know the mechanisms of locks and how to open them without their proper keys. Many locks are simple affairs made to vex only untutored thieves, while others can be complex dwarf-made mechanisms capable of frustrating all but the most determined plunderer.

records.name: Play
records.text: Specialisations: Bagpipe, Lute, Harpsichord, Horn, Violin. Make music with an instrument, hopefully well enough to impress others. A successful Play Test lets you entertain those near enough to hear you.

records.name: Pray
records.text: Invoke, appeal to, or otherwise commune with a deity. For more information on using the Pray Skill to seek divine intervention, see Chapter 7: Religion and Belief.

records.name: Ranged
records.text: Specialisations: Blackpowder, Bow, Crossbow, Engineering, Entangling, Explosives, Sling, Throwing. Anyone can throw a rock, but it takes training and practice to use weapons like bows, pistols, and throwing knives. Each Ranged Specialisation is specific to a group of ranged weapons. If you do not have the Ranged Specialisation for a weapon you wish to use, refer to Chapter 11: Consumer Guide for the penalties you will suffer when using the weapon.

records.name: Research
records.text: Finding useful and frequently obscure knowledge in libraries and other such storehouses of information. Research requires you to have the Read/Write Talent (see page 124). More on what kinds of information you can find and where to start looking can be found on page 150.

records.name: Ride
records.text: Specialisations: Demigryph, Griffon, Horse, Pegasus. Proficiency at riding a particular group of animals; Ride (Horse), for example, will let you ride horses, mules, donkeys, and similar. See page 168 for rules on fighting from the back of a mount.

records.name: Row
records.text: Your prowess at pulling an oar to move a boat through the water. A Row Test is typically only needed when racing, navigating rapids, desperately avoiding bog octopuses, or similar challenging feats.

records.name: Sail
records.text: Operate and manoeuvre a sailing vessel — including knotwork, steering, gauging the wind, and more. Sail is required to operate your own vessel, either alone or as part of a crew. If you are commanding a well trained crew, use Leadership instead.

records.name: Secret Signs
records.text: Specialisations: Grey Order, Guild (Any One), Ranger, Scout, Thief, Vagabond. You have been taught how to use clandestine markings only intelligible to members of a select group. Vagabonds might indicate which homeowners are likely to offer alms, thieves may want to indicate territorial markings or warnings, while scouts may want to warn one another about a dangerous monster’s lair nearby (see page 138).

records.name: Set Trap
records.text: From a simple snare or bear trap, to more spectacular devices like Von Grizzel’s Thief-render, players are unlikely to venture far in the Old World without encountering traps. The Set Trap Skill measures your ability to set and disarm traps of all varieties.

records.name: Sleight of Hand
records.text: Your ability to pick pockets, palm objects, and perform minor tricks of prestidigitation, as well as cheat at games of chance. This Skill is typically Opposed by the Perception Skill of your target.

records.name: Stealth
records.text: Specialisations: Rural, Underground, Urban. Move and hide without being detected, blend into a crowd, or otherwise avoid drawing attention to yourself.

records.name: Swim
records.text: Moving and staying afloat in water. If you have the Swim Skill, you are automatically presumed to be able to swim freely without a Test. But if you find yourself in difficult currents, racing, or fleeing from a ravenous stirpike, a Test will be required.

records.name: Track
records.text: Your ability to follow subtle trails left by others. Track is used to follow and find your target, as well as to hide your trail.

records.name: Trade
records.text: Specialisations: Apothecary, Calligrapher, Chandler, Carpenter, Cook, Embalmer, Engineer, Herbalist, Shipwright, Smith, Tanner. Your ability to practice a trade, to create something or provide a service, as well as your knowledge of the relevant lore surrounding your trade.

records.name: Afraid
records.text: Make an Extended Psychology Test against the target’s Fear. Until accumulated SL equal or exceed its rating, gain no Momentum; its melee attacks against you have Advantage (p. 183).

records.name: Amphibious
records.text: Has Swim; +1 SL to Swim Tests. Full Movement in water.

records.name: Animosity
records.text: On encountering the listed target, make a Psychology Test. Failure: attack socially or physically as appropriate; +1 SL to Fellowship-based Tests to oppose or disparage them (p. 183).

records.name: Belligerent
records.text: Immune to Fear while possessing Momentum.

records.name: Bestial
records.text: No rational thought/language; defends only with Dodge. Shies from fire; fire Wounds inflict Broken. Flees after losing over half Wounds; enters Frenzy instead if cornered, protecting young or Territorial.

records.name: Bite
records.text: Lose Momentum for a Free Attack at Rating Damage (SB already included); uses WS/BS without spending the turn’s Action.

records.name: Blessed
records.text: Can enact the listed deity’s Blessings; Pray at Fellowship +10 (GM may increase).

records.name: Bounce
records.text: When Charging, Leaping or Sprinting, double Movement and leap over intervening terrain and creatures.

records.name: Breath
records.text: The creature’s breath is a powerful weapon. As a ranged attack, they can activate their Breath as a Free Attack, targeting 1 creature they can see within 20 + Toughness Bonus yards and all creatures within SB yards of that target. The attacker makes an Opposed Ballistic Skill/Dodge Test against all targets (the attacker's single roll Opposed by each individual target). If a creature without a BS makes a Breath Attack, count it as having a BS of 30. Losing targets take Rating Damage. Further, if the Trait has any of the following Types in parentheses, apply the associated rules. 0 Acid: Inflicts Damage of TB +4. All weapons and armour carried by the targets suffer 1 Damage. 0 Cold: Inflicts Damage of SB +2. Targets gain a Fatigued Condition; until they lose the Condition, their weapons gain the Slow Flaw. 0 Electricity: Inflicts Damage of SB +2. Damage ignores metal armour. Targets gain a Stunned Condition. 0 Fire: Inflicts Damage of SB +3. Targets gain an Ablaze Condition. 0 Poison: Inflicts Damage of TB +2. Targets gain a Poisoned Condition. 0 Smoke: The area fills with smoke, blocking line of sight and causing Suffocation (page 169) for Toughness Bonus Rounds. The creature is immune to their own Breath. This attack is Magical.

records.name: Champion
records.text: Winning an Opposed Test while defending in melee deals Damage as if attacking.

records.name: Chill Grasp
records.text: Lose Momentum and use an Action: Opposed WS against Dodge or Melee. Win: target loses 1d10 + SL Wounds, ignoring TB and AP. Magical.

records.name: Cold-blooded
records.text: Advantage on Cool Tests. Surprised is not removed the first time it normally would be.

records.name: Constrictor
records.text: Every successful hit inflicts Entangled; may then initiate a Grapple (p. 167).

records.name: Construct
records.text: No Int, WP or Fel; never Tests them, except use T for required WP Tests. Use SB instead of WPB for Wounds. All attacks Magical. Without a controlling spellcaster, or without Territorial, wanders mindlessly.

records.name: Corrosive Blood
records.text: Whenever wounded, all Engaged targets take 1d10 Damage (one roll for all).

records.name: Corruption
records.text: A Corrupting Influence of the listed strength (p. 187).

records.name: Daemonic
records.text: No food, water or air; all attacks Magical. Non-Magical blow: 1d10, Rating+ ignores it and any Critical. Cannot ignore Magical blows this way. At 0 Wounds, returns to Chaos and leaves play.

records.name: Dark Vision
records.text: Sees in darkness as in daylight.

records.name: Disease
records.text: Carries the listed disease; others Test for Contraction as appropriate (p. 179). Whether the carrier suffers its effects is the GM’s choice.

records.name: Distracting
records.text: Living targets within TB yards suffer −2 SL to all Tests. Does not stack with other Distracting creatures.

records.name: Ethereal
records.text: Passes through solid objects. Only Magical attacks can harm it; all its attacks are Magical.

records.name: Fear
records.text: Extended Psychology Test. Until accumulated SL exceed Rating (default 1): no Momentum; attackers gain Advantage in melee (p. 183).

records.name: Fly
records.text: As its Move, fly up to Rating yards, ignoring intervening terrain, obstacles and creatures; may Charge. End landed or airborne; if starting a turn airborne, must Fly or fall (GM decides distance). Against it, measure horizontal range then increase one range step (Extreme becomes unreachable). While flying, −20 to its Ranged Attacks.

records.name: Frenzy
records.text: WP Test to enter: Free Attack each Round, +1 Damage, immune to Psychology. Only attack or move to attack nearest visible enemy; no fleeing/retreat. Ends with no visible enemies or if Stunned or Unconscious; then Fatigued.

records.name: Ghostly Howl
records.text: Once per turn, lose Momentum for a Magical Free Attack. Living hearers within Strength yards gain 3 Deafened and lose 1d10 Wounds ignoring TB/AP; Average (+2 SL) Cool or also Broken.

records.name: Grim
records.text: At the end of its turn, gains Momentum if it has none.

records.name: Hatred
records.text: On meeting target: Psychology Test; failure activates Hatred. Attack by fastest, deadliest means; +1 SL Melee/Ranged against them. Immune to their Intimidate/Fear, not Terror (p. 184).

records.name: Horns
records.text: When Charging into combat, may make a Free Attack at SB +4 Damage.

records.name: Hungry
records.text: After killing/incapacitating living prey or finding a fresh corpse: Average (+2 SL) Cool or feast; lose next Move and Action.

records.name: Immune to Psychology
records.text: Ignores Psychology rules (p. 183).

records.name: Immunity
records.text: Ignores all harm of the listed type, including Critical Wounds.

records.name: Infected
records.text: On causing a living opponent to lose Wounds: Easy (+4 SL) Endurance or contract a Festering Wound (p. 180).

records.name: Infestation
records.text: Opponents suffer −1 SL to hit it in melee.

records.name: Magic Resistance
records.text: Casting Tests for spells affecting it suffer −3 SL. Incompatible with Channelling or Arcane Magic, Bless, Chaos Magic, Invoke, Petty Magic and Witch! Talents (in either direction).

records.name: Magical
records.text: All attacks are Magical and can harm creatures vulnerable only to Magical attacks.

records.name: Many Heads
records.text: Head Criticals stun, kill or render unconscious only when all heads are disabled or similarly affected. With Bite, Horns or Tongue, make as many Free Attacks as healthy heads. With 2+ healthy heads, +2 SL to Perception.

records.name: Mark of Chaos
records.text: Khorne: Frenzy; Etiquette (Followers of Khorne). Animosity towards overt Slaanesh followers (reciprocal while Mark visible). Language (Magick)/Channelling: dispelling only. Career Talents at normal XP: Berserk Charge, Combat Aware, Combat Reflexes, Furious Assault, Implacable, Magic Resistance, Resistance (Magic), Resolute, Strike Mighty Blow, Warrior Born. Nurgle: +10 Toughness; Etiquette (Followers of Nurgle). Animosity towards overt Tzeentch followers; they reciprocate while the Mark is visible. Career purchases at normal XP: Frightening, Hardy, Implacable, Iron Jaw, Menacing, Resistance (Poison), Resistance (Disease), Robust, Tenacious, Very Resilient. Slaanesh: Fearless (Everything); Etiquette (Followers of Slaanesh). Animosity towards overt Khorne followers; they reciprocate while the Mark is visible. Career purchases at normal XP: Attractive, Blather, Careful Strike, Combat Master, Gregarious, Inspiring, Lightning Reflexes, Nimblefingered, Resistant (Poison), Sharp. Tzeentch: Roll 1d10/3 Mutations, rounding up, alternating Mental and Physical. Etiquette (Followers of Tzeentch). Animosity towards overt Nurgle followers; they reciprocate while the Mark is visible. Career purchases at normal XP: Aethyric Attunement, Arcane Magic (Any), Chaos Magic (Tzeentch), Fast Hands, Instinctive Diction, Magical Sense, Petty Magic, Second Sight, War Wizard, Witch!.

records.name: Mental Corruption
records.text: Roll on the Mental Corruption table (p. 189).

records.name: Miracles
records.text: Can enact the listed deity’s Miracles; Pray at Fellowship +10 (GM may increase).

records.name: Mutation
records.text: Roll on the Physical Corruption table (p. 189).

records.name: Night Vision
records.text: See clearly in natural darkness for 20 yards; extend the illumination distance of light sources by 20 yards.

records.name: Painless
records.text: Ignores non-amputation Critical Wound penalties; Conditions still apply.

records.name: Petrifying Gaze
records.text: Lose Momentum and an Action against one visible living target: Opposed BS/Initiative (spellcasters may defend with Language (Magick)). Win: 1 Stunned, +1 per SL after the first. Win by 6+ SL: permanently turn target to stone.

records.name: Regeneration
records.text: Round start: above 0 Wounds, heal 1d10; at 0, heal 1 on 1d10 of 8+. A roll of 10 fully heals one Critical and its penalties/Conditions. Cannot regenerate fire-caused Wounds/Criticals.

records.name: Size
records.text:
This Trait represents creatures whose size differs from the game standard (i.e. roughly human-sized). There are five steps of Size, ranging from Tiny to Monstrous. Size Examples Butterfly, Mouse, Pigeon, Cat, Hawk, Tiny Human Infant Giant Rat, Halfling, Human Child, Average Dwarf, Elf, Human Large Horse, Ogre, Troll Enormous Griffon, Wyvern, Manticore Monstrous Dragon, Giant, Greater Daemon Size Combat Modifiers Large creatures do more Damage when they land a hit. These modifiers don’t apply to Ranged Attacks or extra attacks. NPC profiles already include these modifiers. 
• Small: Damage as normal 
• Average: Damage as normal 
• Large: Damage as normal plus additional SB Damage 
• Enormous: Damage as normal plus additional SB Damage 
• Monstrous: Damage as normal plus additional (2 x SB) Damage Defending Against Big Creatures When fighting a creature of larger size, you suffer a penalty of -2 SL when using Melee to defend in an Opposed Test. It is better to dodge a giant swinging a tree trunk than try to parry it! Fear Agressive creatures cause Fear in those smaller than them. Moving in Combat Creatures ignore the need to Disengage from melee combat with smaller combatants. Opposed Strength During Opposed Strength Tests (and similar), if one creature is 2 or more Size steps larger, they win automatically. If one creature is 1 Size step larger, the smaller creature must score a Critical to contest the roll. If they do, SL are compared as normal. All other results mean the larger creature wins. Outnumbering Larger Creatures Larger creatures count as several creatures for the sake of working out if they are outnumbered in combat. 
• Small: Counts as 1 creature 
• Average: Counts as 1 creature 
• Large: Counts as 2 creatures 
• Enormous: Counts as 3 creatures 
• Monstrous: Counts as 4 creatures So, you would need 4 Size (Average) creatures to outnumber a Size (Large) creature by 2 to 1, or 3 Size (Large) creatures to outnumber a Size (Monstrous) creature by 2 to 1. Conversely, for the sake of larger opponents being daunting enough, they do not themselves count as multiple opponents when working out if they receive a bonus for outnumbering themselves. 2 Size (Large) Ogres outnumber 1 Size (Average) Human 2 to 1, not 4 to 1. Creatures that are larger than their opponents may lose Momentum to make one Stomp as a Free Attack, kicking downwards or otherwise bashing smaller opponents out of the way. This attack has a Damage equal to their Strength Bonus and uses Melee (Brawling). Larger creatures have more Wounds: Size Wounds Small 2 × Toughness Bonus Strength Bonus + (2 × Toughness Average Bonus) + Willpower Bonus (Strength Bonus + (2 × Toughness Large Bonus) + Willpower Bonus) × 2 (Strength Bonus + (2 × Toughness Enormous Bonus) + Willpower Bonus) × 4 (Strength Bonus + (2 × Toughness Monstrous Bonus) + Willpower Bonus) × 8 ADJUSTING A CREATURE’S SIZE if you wish to use Size to make a creature bigger then increase Strength and Toughness by +10 and reduce Agility by -5 per step of size you increase the creature. reverse this if you wish to make a creature smaller. Example: The Giant Spider described in the Bestiary is Size (Small) with a Strength of 15, Toughness of 25, and an Agility of 35. If it were made Size (Large) it would have a Strength of 35, Toughness of 45, and Agility of 25. Its Wounds would increase to 26, its fangs would inflict +5 Damage and its Bite would increase to +6 Damage.

records.name: Skittish
records.text: Spectacular visible magic, thunderclaps or explosions inflict 3 Broken Conditions.

records.name: Spellcaster
records.text: Casts the listed Lore(s). Add Spellcaster/Spellcaster Lord template, or grant Channelling (chosen Wind) at WP +10 and Language (Magick) at Int +10 as Basic Skills (GM may increase).

records.name: Sprinter
records.text: Run Movement ×1.5 when Running.

records.name: Stealthy
records.text: Stealth (Rural) at Agility +10 (GM may increase).

records.name: Striding Gait
records.text: No movement penalties in the listed terrain; +1 SL to Athletics and Stealth there.

records.name: Stupid
records.text: If no nearby ally lacks Stupid, make Easy (+4 SL) Intelligence at each Round’s start. Failure: lose that turn’s Move and Action. Nearby non-Stupid allies prevent this.

records.name: Swarm
records.text: Acts as one creature; ignores Psychology, Engaged restrictions on moving and all Size rules. Each Engaged opponent loses 1 Wound at Round end. Has ×5 normal Wounds and +10 WS; shooting at it gains +40 to hit.

records.name: Tail
records.text: Lose Momentum for a Free Attack at SB +2 Damage; smaller targets losing any Wounds also become Prone.

records.name: Tentacles
records.text: One Free Attack per tentacle at SB +0 Damage. Causing Damage may inflict Entangled and initiate a Grapple with that tentacle. Resolve its Grapple with the tentacle’s Free Attack, not the creature’s Action (p. 167).

records.name: Territorial
records.text: Fights to the death defending its area; normally does not pursue enemies beyond it.

records.name: Terror
records.text: First encounter: Psychology Test; failure gives Broken equal to Rating +1 per negative SL. Causes Fear of same Rating regardless of result (p. 183).

records.name: Tongue
records.text: Lose Momentum for a ranged Free Attack at SB +0 Damage. GM sets range (default 3 yards at Small–Large; 12 for larger). Hit: 1 Entangled; smaller targets dragged into melee. Then release, make a Weapon-Trait Free Attack, or keep wrapped and initiate a Grapple (p. 167).

records.name: Tracker
records.text: Track at Intelligence +10 (GM may increase).

records.name: Trained
records.text: This Trait represents animals that have been trained through the Animal Training Skill. The skills the animal knows are marked in the parentheses. Feel free to create your own Trained skills. Broken: The animal is trained to ignore its Bestial Trait. It receives +2d10 Fellowship. Drive: The animal is trained to pull a coach, cart, plough, buggy, or similar. Entertain: The animal is trained to entertain others. It adds a +10 bonus to appropriate Entertain, Perform, or Play Tests. Fetch: The animal is trained to fetch. This is normally reserved for dogs and similar. Guard: The animal is trained to stay in one place or prowl around as a guard, granting it the Territorial Trait. Home: The animal is trained to return home if it is released or lost. Magic: The animal is trained to ignore Skittish when it comes to magic, which is required for most mounts used by spellcasters. Mount: The animal accepts a rider. Some creatures are especially belligerent, and will not accept a rider without the correct skill. For example, to ride a griffon, you need the Ride (Griffon) Skill. War: The animal is trained for war, gaining +10 Weapon Skill. It can also ignore Skittish for loud noises.

records.name: Undead
records.text: Needs no air, food, water or other life necessities; counts as Undead for spells, Miracles and abilities.

records.name: Unstable
records.text: Round end: Engaged opponent has Momentum and creature has none → driven back; lose 2 Wounds. Destroyed or banished at 0 Wounds.

records.name: Vampiric
records.text: Successful Bite against suitable prey: heal Wounds equal to target’s loss. Blood-drinking is its only healing method.

records.name: Venom
records.text: Causing Wounds inflicts Poisoned. The listed Difficulty applies to Tests to recover from Poisoned, not to avoid it (p. 186).

records.name: Vomit
records.text: If starting the turn Engaged, spend Move and Action: one BS roll opposed by each target’s Dodge within 2 yards. Attacker Easy (+4 SL), defenders Challenging (+0 SL). Losing targets take TB +4 Damage and Stunned; all their carried weapons/armour take 1 Damage. Once per 12 hours.

records.name: Wallcrawler
records.text: Full Movement on suitable vertical surfaces and ceilings; automatically passes Climb Tests.

records.name: Ward
records.text: After any blow, roll 1d10: Rating+ ignores the blow, including Criticals.

records.name: Web
records.text: Each successful hit inflicts 1 Entangled, with Strength equal to Rating (p. 186).

records.name: Arboreal
records.text: Add the creature's Agility Bonus in SL to Stealth and Climb Tests in woodlands.

records.name: Die Hard
records.text: All Critical Wounds can be healed. For Toughness Bonus Rounds after death, at the start of each Round make a Challenging (+0 SL) Endurance Test. On success, return to life with 1 Wound.
records.adaptation: User-supplied older-edition definition retained; no direct Fifth Edition equivalent.

records.name: Corrupting Vomit
records.text: Those hit by a Chaos Troll’s vomit risk exposure to Corruption (Moderate).

records.name: Rotten Regeneration
records.text: Use core Regeneration, but the Wounds restored are 1d10 divided by 2, rounded down (Tribes and Tribulations p. 88).

records.name: Bileful Vomit
records.text: The Troll’s Vomit follows core Stream of Corruption: CN: 9 Range: Special Target: Special Duration: Instant Your maw distends horrifically before you vomit forth a foul stream of diseased filth and horror. Immediately make an Unopposed Acid- and Poison-type Breath attack (see page 357). It counts as a magic missile with a Damage equal to your Toughness Bonus, and it ignores Armour Points. Further, any targets that take more than their TB in Wounds must pass a Challenging (+0 SL) Endurance Test or contract Blood Rot (see page 179).

records.name: That’s No Mound
records.text: The Troll has Stealthy only while it has not moved or taken an Action.

records.name: Sated
records.text: After consuming a creature of Average Size or larger in peace, the Hungry Troll template no longer applies.

records.name: Starving
records.text: If the Hungry Troll does not eat within 24 hours it begins to suffer Starvation.

records.name: Water Wise
records.text: While within a body of water, the River Troll Hag does not suffer from Stupid. Stupid otherwise remains active.

records.name: Purple Skullback Bite
records.text: A creature wounded and Poisoned by this bite takes an Average (+2 SL) Cool Test or gains 1 Corruption point. A Forest Goblin Shaman still takes damage and poison, but for 2d10 hours gains a printed +2d10 bonus to Channelling and Language (Magick), and may reroll Waaagh! Miscast results. Situational bonuses are not added permanently.
records.adaptation: Printed Average (+20) uses core Average (+2 SL); current Venom inflicts Poisoned on Wounds without an avoidance Test.

records.name: Lure of the Lurkerfish
records.text: The gently oscillating blue- green lights seen by the riverbank at dusk and dawn are sometimes mistaken for fireflies. Any Character passing a Hard (−2 SL) Lore (Riverways) Test will know that these are likely to be the lures of Lurkerfish. Those who fail the Lore Test must make an Easy (+4 SL) Cool Test or become beguiled by the sight and unable to perform any action except moving towards the light — effectively acquiring the Unconscious Condition.
records.adaptation: Printed Test Difficulty uses current SL modifiers.

records.name: Slimy
records.text: Latch-eels can produce a surprising quantity of slime, in or out of the water. If a Latch-eel is ever Grappled by an opponent, it may make a Toughness Test. If it succeeds, it produces a clump of slime, benefiting from +4 SL to subsequent Tests to break free. The opponent must make a Challenging (+0 SL) Athletics Test. Failure means that slime has covered their face, and the opponent must either release the Latch-eel or start to suffer suffocation (WFRP, page 181).

records.name: Love the Light
records.text: Daggerfish are attracted to light. Attempts to use fire to deter them only encourages them further. Whilst they possess the Bestial trait, they do not shy from fire or take Broken Conditions from being struck by flaming attacks.

records.name: Immersion
records.text: The Sea Elemental may attempt to immerse its opponents by making a Grapple. If the Sea Elemental inflicts an Entangled Condition on its opponent, it draws them into its own body. The immersed character suffers from Suffocation as detailed on WFRP, page 181. They may attempt to escape by freeing themselves from the Entangled Condition as if they were Grappled by the Sea Elemental, making Opposed Strength Tests against its Strength of 59 to break free. However, the Sea Elemental does not need to actively maintain the Grapple — it may act as if the immersed character were not there and does not count as being Engaged.

records.name: Fire Resistant
records.text: Sea Elementals never suffer from Ablaze Conditions.

records.name: Mindless Spellcaster
records.text: Sea Elementals may use their Strength Characteristic for the purpose of casting spells and channelling.

records.name: Boat Crusher
records.text: The Gargantuan may attempt to constrict a vessel of Size Large or smaller. To constrict a vessel, it must spend one turn wrapping itself about the vessel for every 10 points of Size the vessel possesses. Once the vessel is wrapped up, the Gargantuan starts to squeeze — making an Extended Opposed Strength Test against the boat’s Toughness. Once the SL reaches the boat’s Wounds, the boat shatters, reduced to a mass of flotsam. During this time, the boat’s crew may attack the Gargantuan or attempt to lever it from the boat. Attacks that inflict more than 7 Wounds may cause the Gargantuan to let go if it fails a subsequent Average (+2 SL) Cool Test. Levering the Gargantuan requires making an Opposed Strength Test against the creature. A result of 0 to 4 SL prevents it from squeezing the boat that turn, and a result of 5 SL or more forces it to release the boat.
records.adaptation: Printed Test Difficulty uses current SL modifiers.

records.name: Electrical Discharge
records.text: If the creature successfully Grapples an opponent, then at the start of its subsequent turns, the creature can spend 1 Momentum to deliver an electric shock to the Grappled character. The electrical discharge inflicts a hit of 10 Damage which ignores non- magical metal armour. Any Character taking Wounds from the electrical attack must also pass a Difficult (−1 SL) Endurance Test or suffer a Stunned Condition. The Gargantuan cannot make electrical attacks with impunity. Each time it uses the attack, it must make an Average (+2 SL) Endurance Test. Failure indicates that it suffers a Fatigued Condition. Whilst the Gargantuan is under the effects of a Fatigued Condition, electrical discharge attacks only inflict Damage 6 hits which ignore non-magical metal armour. The Gargantuan may also discharge electricity when it has Grappled a boat. This does no damage against the boat, but the crew all receive a jolt, suffering a Damage 6 hit (reduced to a Damage 3 hit if the Gargantuan has a Fatigued Condition).
records.adaptation: Printed Test Difficulty uses current SL modifiers. Printed Advantage uses Momentum.

records.name: Whale Bane
records.text: All Fanged Maw attacks have core Venom (Difficult −1 SL recovery): causing Wounds inflicts Poisoned; the Difficulty applies to recovery.
records.adaptation: Uses full Fifth Edition Venom rather than the older on-hit interpretation.

records.name: Syreen’s Call
records.text: As an action the Syreen may sing its luring song. Characters within a number of yards equal to the Syreen’s Initiative must make an Difficult (−1 SL) Cool Test or become beguiled by the call and unable to perform any action except moving towards the Syreen — effectively acquiring the Unconscious Condition.
records.adaptation: Printed Test Difficulty uses current SL modifiers.

records.name: Resistant to Cold
records.text: Any weapon, spell, or effect that inflicts damage or impairment due to cold will likely have a reduced impact on an Orb Leviathan. It may make an Endurance Test to ignore any ill effects from cold and ice.

records.name: Lure of the Leviathan
records.text: The first sign of an approaching attack by an Orb Leviathan is a lambent yellow light drifting slowly underwater. Any Character passing a Hard (−2 SL) Lore (Oceans) Test will have heard about the lure of the Orb Leviathan, and may look away before it takes effect. Those who fail the Lore Test must succeed on an Easy (+4 SL) Cool Test or acquire the Stunned Condition.
records.adaptation: Printed Test Difficulty uses current SL modifiers.

records.name: Devastating Assault
records.text: When a Black Leviathan charges a ship, it causes a collision with a CR of 50.

records.name: On a Different Scale
records.text: The Black Leiviathan possesses the Bestial Trait and can be scared by fire. However, guttering torches are too small to attract its notice, let alone scare it. To benefit from the frightening qualities of fire, the blaze must be the size and intensity of a large bonfire; anything less isn’t going to concern the Black Leviathan. When considering the psychological impact of other sources of Fear and Terror, the GM should consider that unless the source is something the Black Leviathan should respect in terms of size, it is unlikely to bother the beast. Unearthly as Daemonettes, Zombies, and wizards with flaming heads may be, the Black Leviathan regards them all as fish food.

records.name: Marine Creature
records.text: The creature is at home in the ocean and unsuited to life on land. Its printed profile assumes an aquatic environment and it moves its full Movement in water. Out of water, Movement drops to 1 and all its Tests suffer −2 SL. It must be regularly doused with water or begin to suffocate (core Suffocation).
